This document provides an interview report template for interviewers, aiming to systematically evaluate and score candidates based on multiple dimensions such as professional skills, experience fit, soft skills, cultural fit, and growth potential, grounded in interview facts.
The interview report requires interviewers to evaluate candidates based on facts discussed during the interview, avoid subjective impressions, and use a scoring standard from 1 to 5, where 1 means not meeting expectations, 3 means basically meeting expectations, and 5 means far exceeding expectations.
The professional skills dimension should assess whether the candidate possesses the professional knowledge and technical abilities required for the role, and whether their problem-solving approach is clear and logical, while identifying their strengths and weaknesses.
The experience fit dimension should assess how well the candidate's work experience matches the role, and whether they have cases of successfully handling similar challenges, listing highlights and concerns separately.
The soft skills dimension should assess the candidate’s communication, teamwork, learning ability, adaptability, and conflict resolution abilities.
The cultural fit dimension should assess the candidate’s alignment with the mission, values, and team culture of an AI startup, as well as the interest they showed in the company during the interview.
The growth potential dimension should comment on the capabilities and potential the candidate demonstrated in their work.
The report should list at least 5 of the most critical interviewer questions and candidate answers from the interview.
The overall evaluation section should summarize the candidate’s strengths and highlights, shortcomings or risks, and provide an overall impression.
The final recommendation section should specify whether to recommend hiring (with four levels), whether to proceed to the next interview round, and any special observations or supplemental training plans that may be needed after hiring.

name: Function Manual Interviews for PROCESS DIGITIZATION - DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION
author: Velum
description: Fill in the record sheet and order speeches by turns. Generate an index by script and excerpts for checking.
body:
Organization of records of the second conversation round with teacher coordinators of the Educational Technology Centers (CTEs) of the Manaus municipal network, preparing the material for subsequent Discursive Textual Analysis (ATD) by Moraes and Galiazzi (2016), focusing on faithfulness, context, and traceability.
Research “Contemporary educational practices in continuing teacher education: pedagogical innovations with digital technologies at SEMED-Manaus,” with the general objective of analyzing the repercussions of digital technologies on the continuing education of SEMED Manaus teachers, having as main participants CTE coordinators linked to training by the Educational Technology Management (GTE) and differentiating CTE coordinators, GTE trainers, and the researcher.
Recording of school practices only as experiences reported by the participant, without characterization as direct observation by the researcher, and absence of school visits as a component of the study.
Record identification with fields to be filled by the researcher (type of record, recording code, date, place, duration, participant codes, record context) and inclusion of the full semi-structured script when available, with provisional use of axes (education and trajectory; appropriation/adaptation of practices with digital technologies from GTE training; facilities and difficulties in adaptation and multiplication) and explicit signaling when these axes are used.
Faithfulness to speeches with preservation of transcription wording (expressions, hesitations, relevant repetitions, doubts, and contradictions), without academicization, without completing interrupted excerpts, with marking of points requiring audio checking, distinction between literal excerpt, descriptive synthesis, and provisional observation, and prohibition of inventing participants, events, feelings, results, references, time markings, or non-recorded paralinguistic elements.
Use of timestamps only when they exist in the material and, in their absence, record as “time not available,” without attributing laughter, pauses, intonations, or overlapping voices when not in the transcription.
Confidentiality with consistent use of codes defined by the researcher, adoption of provisional labels (e.g., “Speaker A”) when identification is not secure with indication of need for checking, prohibition of associating names to voices by assumption or transferring identifications between recordings, anonymization of names of people, schools, and identifiable data with markers (e.g., [name omitted], [school omitted]) and non-reproduction of contacts or personal data unnecessary to the research.
Response structure with record sheet containing code, type of recording, date, place, duration, identified participants, and missing information, ensuring explicit recording of gaps.
Record organized in chronological order maintaining the sequence of the conversation and, for each intervention, turn identifier (e.g., RC02-T001), speaker code, timestamp when available, speech as per the transcription, and signaling of doubt/interruption/anonymization, also preserving the researcher’s interventions and providing for division into numbered parts when exceeding the response limit with indication of the interruption point.
Index of speeches by the script linking turns to each question or topic and brief descriptive synthesis, allowing association of a speech to more than one topic without altering its original location, including spontaneous issues, questions without answers, partial answers, and excerpts without clear relation to the script, without forcing framing into the expected axes.
Recording interactions between participants identifying complements, questions, confirmations, and disagreements, indicating turns and content, without interpreting silence as agreement and without turning an individual statement into group consensus.
Suggestion of candidate excerpts for checking and subsequent unitization, presented as provisional in a table with excerpt code (e.g., RC02-R001), origin turn(s), participant, available timestamp, literal excerpt, necessary context, provisional descriptive title, possible relation to the script, and doubts for checking, selecting excerpts with comprehensible meaning and preserved context, avoiding mechanical fragmentation and avoiding final categories, automatic association to theories, or counting frequency as a measure of importance.
Questions for the researcher’s reading formulated as reflection questions supported by excerpts and indicating their codes, considering differences in experiences, tensions, contradictions, reported changes, and unexpected issues, without presenting answers as conclusions.
Pending checks listing speakers with uncertain identification, excerpts requiring audio listening, doubtful terms or acronyms, missing information, risks of loss of context, unprocessed parts, and situations where synthesis may have simplified the speech.
Treatment of complementary audios from GTE trainers as a complementary source separate from the conversation round, organized by audio and trainer code, training context when informed, content in chronological order, literal excerpts with location, separate descriptive synthesis, and pending checks, without treating the trainer’s speech as a CTE coordinator’s response, without using it as automatic confirmation of the conversation round reports, and explicitly stating when the record is partial without generalization to the entire GTE training proposal.
Final guidance prioritizing faithfulness, context, and traceability, with organization that allows locating each excerpt in the transcription and, when possible, in the original audio, maintaining titles and syntheses with clarity and moderate formality, preserving speeches without adaptation to the researcher’s style, and keeping interpretive suggestions as provisional and dependent on checking and the researcher’s decision.

name: Ethics Committee
author: Velum
description: Creates a story plan by days and quantity from a voice technical task. Takes into account the goal and tone.
body:
The main goal is to transform a voice technical task (TS) into a structured marketing story plan for Instagram, which will lead the audience to the target action.
It is necessary to strictly adhere to the voiced TS regarding the number of days and stories, without adding unnecessary elements such as links or materials if they are not specified, and to focus on an average story length for oral delivery.
It is important to think like a marketer and scriptwriter for warming-up campaigns, using relevant tools such as strong hooks, triggers, FOMO, intrigue, and native selling, so that each story works towards the overall goal.
If the TS provides information about the blogger, their presentation style, character, blog theme, and communication manner must be taken into account so that the story text sounds natural.
When creating a warming-up scenario, it is necessary to consider the previous context, continuing the logical line of previous days and stories to avoid repetition and build a unified chain.
If the TS specifies a product or service for the warming-up, the entire scenario must lead specifically to them, revealing relevant meanings, advantages, and addressing audience pains and objections.
The warming-up must be adapted to a specific blogger so that the text sounds authentic and the style matches their image — gentle, emotional, expert, lifestyle, or provocative.
Each story must have a specific meaning, work towards an overall goal (sales, hype, interest), and be part of a coherent scenario, not just a set of separate messages.
The final result should be presented in a clear structure: day header, a short sentence about the day's essence, and sequentially numbered stories with detailed text for the blogger, in a copy-friendly format.
Content quality requirements for each story include natural language for the blogger, emotional plausibility, specificity, adherence to the set tone, ease for voice recording, and sufficient detail for the blogger to understand what to say.
If the TS includes a sales task, elements that address audience pain, build trust, highlight product value, and include a call to action should be incorporated; if it is only storytelling, the focus should be on intrigue, emotional development, and maintaining attention.
The most important task is to accurately execute the TS regarding the number of days, stories, and specified materials, combining this with marketing thinking to achieve the stated goal.

name: Counseling Assistant ~ Jr Stylist
author: Velum
description: From a transcription, create a structured and factual MMA PRO BTP collection. "Not specified" if absent.
body:
The main objective is to create a structured form, the "MMA INFORMATION COLLECTION – PRO BTP CONTRACT", to collect the necessary information for establishing the Special Conditions of a Property Damage insurance contract for BTP activities, strictly complying with MMA reference documents.
Insured identification requires collecting their company name, legal form, establishment date, SIREN/SIRET numbers, the identity and function of their legal representatives, as well as the total number of legal entities to be insured.
It is fundamental to precisely declare the company's activities, distinguishing main, secondary, subcontracted activities, and those undeclared but necessary, and to specify whether works are subject to decennial insurance obligation or carried out as subcontracting.
Economic and operational data to be collected include global annual turnover (excluding tax), financial year, total workforce, presence of an accountant or collaborating spouse.
Operating locations must be identified, specifying the main site's address, its developed area, occupancy status (tenant or owner), its potential location in a shopping center, and whether its use is exclusively administrative.
For property damage coverage, it is necessary to define the capital for operational movable assets according to a predefined declaration method, as well as the value of real estate assets, fittings, and archives, and to report the presence of sensitive materials.
The assessment of prevention and technical characteristics of the building is an insurability condition that covers the type of construction, the heating system, the annual verification of electrical installations, and the presence and condition of fire fighting means (extinguishers, RIA).
The analysis of claims over the last 36 months, an MMA acceptance criterion, requires the total number of claims and their detail by nature (water damage, theft, fire, natural disaster), as well as any prior cancellation or collective proceedings.
The insurable liabilities section aims to determine whether the contract should cover Civil Liability (operating and professional) and Decennial Liability, specifying the context of the works (on existing structures, intermediate damages, etc.).
It is necessary to define the geographical scope of construction sites (France, EU) and specific intervention methods, such as working in a temporary consortium of companies (GME) or using modular shelters.
The form allows for listing additional guarantees discussed with the client, such as loss of operation, theft on construction site, machinery breakdown, or professional legal protection.
A section is dedicated to identifying points of vigilance and potential exclusions, particularly undeclared activities, identified prevention failures, or risks not insurable by MMA, which might require specific validation.
The collection concludes with the definition of actions to be followed for the MMA agency, including additional information and documents to request, the necessity of a risk visit, and the orientation for the pricing study.
An operational summary of a maximum of five lines must be drafted to enable a quick decision by the General Agent or the underwriting department, adhering to strict rules of factual and contractual reporting.

name: Expert Audit for Unhealthy Conditions
author: Velum
description: Turn a transcript into a hiring report with strengths, risks, and follow-ups. Job-relevant, fact-based.
body:
This document provides a comprehensive template for analyzing interviews with Registered Behavior Technician (RBT) and Behavior Technician (BT) candidates who will provide Applied Behavior Analysis (ABA) services to children with autism, aiming to produce a structured hiring report based solely on the interview transcript.
The analysis is guided by a five-point rating scale to assess candidate competency, ranging from "Exceptional" to "High Risk/Not Demonstrated," which must be applied consistently across all evaluated areas.
The process begins by documenting the candidate's basic information, including credentials, experience, availability, and compensation requests, to establish a foundational profile.
An executive summary must be created to provide a concise overview of the candidate's general impression, experience, motivation, understanding of the role, readiness, primary strengths, and risks, culminating in an overall assessment rating.
Professional and clinical skills are evaluated across key domains, including the candidate's understanding of the RBT/BT role, ABA knowledge, data collection abilities, problem-solving judgment in clinical scenarios, and safety awareness.
The candidate's relevant experience is analyzed for its alignment with the position, focusing on the length and type of experience with ABA, autism, and specific clinical challenges, and assessing the quality of examples provided.
Soft skills and workplace functioning are assessed, covering communication, teamwork, learning ability, adaptability, conflict resolution, and emotional regulation, based on observable evidence from the interview.
The candidate's fit for working with children with autism is specifically evaluated by examining their respect for neurodiversity, use of dignified language, understanding of behavioral functions, and avoidance of punitive approaches.
Readiness for managing challenging behaviors is assessed by evaluating the candidate's comfort level, willingness to follow behavior plans and seek help, and ability to remain neutral and maintain client dignity.
The template requires an evaluation of the candidate's reliability, attendance, and work habits by examining evidence related to punctuality, schedule consistency, and adherence to documentation and communication procedures.
A critical assessment of the candidate's understanding and adherence to ethics, confidentiality, and professional boundaries is required, flagging any disclosures of inappropriate practices like social media posts about clients or dual relationships.
The candidate's cultural and organizational fit is evaluated based on their alignment with an organization that values consistency, data-driven decisions, direct feedback, and accountability, while avoiding biases related to personality or background.
Growth potential is assessed by rating the candidate's capacity for development in areas like RBT certification, competency mastery, and potential for advanced roles, supported by evidence from the interview.
A detailed behavioral interview analysis is conducted to identify observable verbal patterns, including ownership versus blame, specificity of answers, consistency, response to pressure, and interaction style, with confidence levels assigned to each conclusion.
Observable language and interaction patterns are documented, focusing on repeated language, emphasized topics, response structure, and tone indicators to understand the candidate's communication style and potential job-related motivations.
The analysis identifies job-relevant motivational needs, such as stability or recognition, supported by evidence, and considers how these needs might manifest at work and how they can be appropriately managed.
A risk analysis is conducted to identify and classify red flags related to clinical safety, reliability, integrity, supervision, and boundaries, distinguishing confirmed concerns from those requiring clarification.
The candidate's concrete strengths and protective factors, such as honest self-assessment, strong data orientation, and respectful language, are identified and supported with transcript evidence.
A list of all material information requiring verification before a hiring decision is made must be compiled, including credentials, employment history, and references.
Based on the analysis, targeted second-interview and reference-check questions are generated to probe weaknesses, inconsistencies, and missing information.
A plan for training and supervision is outlined for potentially successful candidates, detailing required training and a structured onboarding process for the first 90 days.
An overall risk classification (Low, Moderate, High) and a final hiring recommendation (e.g., Proceed to Offer, Do Not Proceed) are made, supported by evidence and including specific conditions and a five-line summary of strengths, risks, fit, potential, and the final decision.
The final report must adhere to strict writing standards, being professional, fact-based, and free from unsupported psychological conclusions or discriminatory analysis.

name: Parent FTF (Child Welfare Case Management Narrative)
author: Velum
description: Paste transcript; get third-person parent contact note. Uses required headers and court-ready wording.
body:
Task is to convert an audio recording of a face-to-face visit with a parent into a complete professional Texas child welfare case note in Sarah Gipson’s documentation style.
Writing requirements specify third-person narrative, chronological order, lengthy paragraphs, parent name usage, “Personnel Gipson” for the caseworker, court-ready documentation, relevant parent statements, observed demeanor, and no invented information.
Required wording includes standard CPS documentation phrases such as “Personnel Gipson observed,” “The parent reports,” “Personnel Gipson reviewed,” and “No concerns were identified at this time.”
Required document format begins with “MONTHLY REQUIRED FTF CONTACT WITH PARENT” and includes contact details for worker, date, time, client time, purpose, method, announcement status, location, others contacted, and principals or collaterals contacted.
Initial contact narrative must document arrival, present individuals, environment, parent appearance, demeanor, mood, affect, interaction with the worker, residence observations, seating arrangements, and cooperation level.
Home environment and stability narrative must address residence details, length of stay, housing stability, household composition, sleeping arrangements, utilities, safety, cleanliness, placement or visitation adequacy, moves, housing plans, and caseworker suitability observations.
Employment and financial stability narrative must cover employment, employer, work hours, finances, employment barriers, education, vocational training, income, benefits, transportation, employment goals, and progress since the last visit.
Family Plan of Service review must document completed, pending, and missed services; barriers; parent understanding; caseworker education; recommendations; signatures if discussed; and upcoming requirements.
Parenting services and skills narrative must address parenting classes, progress, knowledge gained, use of learned skills, child development understanding, protective capacities, strengths, improvement areas, and insight into child needs.
Mental health and therapeutic services narrative must cover counseling, psychiatric care, medication management, skills training, diagnoses, compliance, treatment progress, recommendations, and barriers.
Substance abuse services narrative must document assessment, treatment, drug testing, sobriety progress, recovery supports, and recommendations when applicable, or state that no substance abuse concerns were discussed.
Visitation and family contact narrative must describe parent-child visits, frequency, supervision, parent engagement, child responses, concerns, requested changes, upcoming visits, transportation, increased visitation requirements, and sibling visitation.
Permanency goal and case status narrative must address each child’s permanency goal, parent understanding, reunification efforts, relative or fictive kin options, adoption, conservatorship, concerns, progress, barriers, court expectations, and caseworker guidance.
Court and legal updates narrative must document hearings, court orders, legal requirements, parent compliance, reviewed documents, deadlines, and legal expectations explained.
Emotional functioning and parent response narrative must describe emotional presentation, stressors, strengths, concerns, insight, accountability, reactions, emotional responses, and motivation toward reunification.
Transportation and support systems narrative must cover transportation resources, license status, vehicle ownership, insurance, registration, family supports, community supports, informal supports, and needed resources.
Child safety discussion must document safety topics, protective capacities, identified concerns, supervision expectations, discipline, child-specific concerns, recommendations, and parent understanding of safety needs.
Caseworker assessment must summarize service compliance, parenting progress, employment, housing, mental health, visitation, reunification readiness, strengths, barriers, next steps, safety assessment, and overall permanency progress.
Ending documentation must include reviewed documents, signatures, photos, home tour, assigned follow-up tasks, resources, referrals, future appointments or hearings, and how the visit concluded.
Completed note must read as a detailed monthly parent contact narrative by Sarah Gipson and be ready for immediate use in official child welfare documentation.

name: Child Forensic Interview - Kansas Child First protocol
author: Velum
description: Summarize 1:1 supervisor interviews in a neutral, structured format. Covers strengths, gaps, barriers.
body:
The primary purpose is to provide a structured template for summarizing a one-on-one supervisor interview at EOO University, focusing on identifying team strengths, issues, skill gaps, and training needs to inform training design and executive reporting.
The process begins by capturing basic interview details, including the supervisor's name, department, role, number of reports, interview date, and facilitator's name.
A department snapshot is required to provide an overview of its work, environment, and performance realities.
Team strengths are to be summarized, covering capabilities, collaboration, professionalism, and technical skills, noting whether these are widespread or concentrated.
The summary should identify any employees performing above expectations and their standout qualities.
It must pinpoint the top 1-3 priority issues affecting the team, detailing the issue, its practical manifestation, operational impact, frequency, and scope.
Skill gaps and development needs are to be cataloged across technical, operational, administrative, compliance, communication, leadership, planning, and analytical categories.
The template requires summarizing areas where the supervisor provides repeated coaching or correction.
Department-specific challenges, such as regulatory obligations, workload demands, and technical complexity, need to be described.
Recent changes that have increased skill demands, like policy updates or reorganizations, must be summarized.
Barriers limiting employee performance should be identified and distinguished between those solvable by training and those that are not.
The summary must assess leadership readiness and advancement potential within the team, including bench strength and necessary skills for succession.
Factors limiting employee advancement, both individual and structural, are to be specified.
The interview should capture the training formats that are most and least effective for the team, along with the reasons why.
Future skill needs for the department over the next 1-3 years should be summarized, distinguishing between immediate and long-term requirements.
Any specific training or development opportunities requested for the team or support requested by the supervisor for staff development must be captured.
A clear distinction must be made between issues that can be solved through training and non-training issues that are structural, operational, or policy-related.
The top three recommended training priorities for the department need to be identified, including why each matters, who it affects, and its urgency.
For each top priority, a suggested training type and delivery approach should be recommended based on the interview findings.
The summary should identify any operational risk signals mentioned, such as compliance issues, repeated errors, or burnout.
Leadership development signals, like the presence of emerging leaders, skill gaps, or a weak succession pipeline, need to be noted.
The template includes a section for capturing 1-5 notable or revealing quotes from the supervisor.
A concise, report-ready summary is required, with single sentences covering department strengths, main skill gaps, leadership readiness, top development need, and the nature of the biggest performance barriers.
Optionally, internal scores on a 1-5 scale for skill gap severity, training fixability, leadership readiness, and operational risk can be provided with a brief justification if sufficient evidence exists.

name: Interview Filter - Consulting
author: Velum
description: Paste a transcript. Get a neutral, factual summary with clear attribution, key facts, and follow-ups.
body:
This document provides a template and guidelines for creating a professional, objective, and factual summary of a recorded insurance or Special Investigations Unit (SIU) interview, emphasizing that the audio recording and transcript are the authoritative sources.
The summary must be based solely on information expressly stated in the interview, avoiding any assumptions, inferences, speculation, embellishments, or credibility judgments.
Interviewee Identification: Capture the interviewee's full name, role in the claim, relationship to involved parties, contact information, address, and employment details as stated.
Recording and Consent: Document whether the interviewee was informed about the recording and if they provided verbal consent or acknowledgment.
Background and Relationship Information: Summarize relevant background details provided by the interviewee, including relationships between parties, living arrangements, and ownership or authorized use of the property involved.
Facts of Loss: Present a detailed chronological account of the loss event from the interviewee's perspective, including the date, time, location, conditions, and sequence of events before, during, and after the incident.
Vehicle, Property, or Equipment Information: When relevant, summarize details on the ownership, rental status, permission for use, pre- and post-loss condition, and any described damage to vehicles, property, or equipment.
Occupants and Other Involved Persons: Identify all individuals mentioned as being present, involved, or having knowledge of the loss, including drivers, passengers, witnesses, and first responders.
Injuries and Medical Treatment: If applicable, summarize reported injuries, the onset of symptoms, medical treatment received, providers visited, and any work restrictions discussed.
Police, Emergency, and Official Response: Detail any discussions about the involvement of police, fire, or EMS, including reports, citations, arrests, and statements made to law enforcement.
Witnesses and Evidence: List any potential evidence mentioned, such as witnesses, photos, videos, surveillance footage, documents, and electronic records, noting who reportedly possesses the evidence.
Prior and Post-Loss Communications: Summarize relevant communications the interviewee had with other parties, insurance carriers, attorneys, or witnesses regarding the incident.
Material Admissions, Denials, and Significant Statements: Isolate key statements from the interviewee that could significantly impact the investigation, such as admissions or denials related to vehicle operation, permission, presence, or substance use.
Discrepancies or Areas Requiring Clarification: Objectively identify factual discrepancies, ambiguities, or incomplete answers from the interview, such as conflicting timelines or an inability to recall key information.
Investigative Leads and Follow-Up: List actionable investigative leads that arise directly from the interview, such as additional witnesses to contact, records to obtain, or video to seek.
Key Quotations: Include a very limited number of brief, direct quotations only when the exact wording is materially significant to the investigation.
Overall Statement Summary: Conclude with a high-level paragraph summarizing the interviewee's relationship to the claim, their general account of the loss, key issues, identified evidence, and any unresolved factual matters.

name: Annual individual performance review
author: Velum
description: Paste the transcript. Get a scored, quote-backed review of new-business sales fit, risks, next steps.
body:
This document provides a comprehensive framework for an experienced Talent Acquisition Director and Sales Leader to analyze an interview transcript for a Business Development Manager role, focusing on assessing the candidate's suitability for new business sales in an SME assistive technology company.
The Executive Summary section requires a concise overview of the candidate, including their overall impression, key strengths and concerns, likelihood of success, and the recommended next step.
The Candidate Profile Summary section outlines the need to summarize the candidate's career history, relevant industry and new business sales experience (specifically in healthcare, education, or public sectors), and their level of seniority.
The New Business Sales Assessment section requires a detailed evaluation and scoring (1-10) of the candidate's capabilities in prospecting, pipeline management, outbound activities, managing complex sales cycles, qualifying opportunities, negotiation, closing, and achieving targets, supported by evidence and commentary.
The Consultative Selling Capability section involves assessing skills such as discovery, active listening, understanding customer needs, articulating value, solution-selling, stakeholder engagement, and selling on value over price, culminating in an overall score out of 10.
The Cultural and SME Fit assessment evaluates the candidate's suitability for a small-to-medium enterprise environment by considering adaptability, self-sufficiency, pace, ownership, comfort with ambiguity, collaboration style, and cultural alignment, resulting in a scored rationale.
The Assistive Technology Sector Fit section assesses the candidate's empathy for end-users, understanding of accessibility, motivation for the sector, ability to learn a specialist market, and alignment with company values, which is also scored with a supporting rationale.
The Behavioural Competency Assessment section mandates evaluating the strength (Strong/Moderate/Weak) of traits like resilience, drive, accountability, initiative, learning agility, emotional intelligence, commercial acumen, and problem-solving, based on supporting evidence.
The Risk Analysis section requires identifying and classifying potential risks (LOW/MEDIUM/HIGH) related to the candidate's experience, skills, and cultural fit, detailing the evidence, severity, potential impact, and suggested mitigation for each.
The Red Flags section is for identifying warning signs such as an inability to evidence achievements, inconsistent answers, blaming others, poor preparation, lack of accountability, job hopping, inflated claims, or weak motivation, with examples from the transcript.
The Interview Gaps section requires identifying areas not fully explored during the interview and suggesting additional questions for a subsequent interview stage.
The Scorecard section provides a template for a quantitative summary, scoring the candidate out of 10 across twelve specific competencies and calculating an overall score out of 100.
The Final Recommendation section requires a single, decisive recommendation (Strong Hire, Hire, Hold for Further Assessment, or No Hire) with a clear explanation of the reasoning.
The Confidence Rating section asks for a declaration of confidence (High, Medium, or Low) in the final recommendation, supported by an explanation, with all conclusions based strictly on evidence from the transcript.

name: Infant Child FTF In Home (Child Welfare Case Management Narrative)
author: Velum
description: Use infant visit recording to draft a third-person case note with required headers and observations.
body:
Primary purpose is to provide comprehensive guidelines and formatting requirements for structuring an objective, detailed child welfare case management narrative regarding an in-home monthly face-to-face visit with an infant.
Foundational writing requirements mandate a third-person narrative in chronological order without bullet points, emphasizing objective documentation of environmental conditions, caregiver statements, and direct caseworker observations.
Standardized vocabulary and phrasing centered around a designated caseworker name are required to maintain consistent, professional descriptions of observations, caregiver communications, and child well-being assessments.
Documentation must begin with standardized metadata headers logging logistical contact details, followed by an initial narrative detailing the home environment, child physical appearance, mood, hygiene, safety conditions, and immediate caregiver interactions.
Assessment of infant developmental progress must capture physical milestones, communication abilities, social-emotional development, and associated caregiver or caseworker observations regarding growth.
Family visitation records must capture the frequency, supervision status, family involvement, and the child's reactions to visits, or provide an explicit explanation if no visitation occurs.
Placement and safety narratives must comprehensively evaluate caregiver attachment, household safety, safe sleep practices, sleeping arrangements, and the availability of age-appropriate supplies such as formula and clothing.
Educational and therapeutic documentation must detail daycare attendance, developmental benefits, and specialized therapies, or explicitly state the absence of these services while noting ongoing developmental monitoring.
Permanency goal and status records must detail primary and concurrent goals, current case status, court proceedings, service plan progress, and updates regarding reunification or adoption plans.
Medical and dental assessments must track physical health, medical compliance, well-child visits, nutritional needs, weight gain, sleep patterns, physical observations, illnesses, and physician recommendations.
Infant adjustment and well-being assessments must address daily routines, temperament, self-soothing abilities, emotional presentation, and social exposure through community participation and interactions with household members.
A standard mandatory statement must be utilized to explicitly note that transitional planning is not applicable due to the child's infant age.
Final documentation requires a comprehensive professional assessment summarizing child safety, placement stability, health, and progress, concluding with confirmation of photos obtained, forms reviewed, and sleeping arrangements observed.

name: interview informan
author: Velum
description: Turn notes into a scannable brief with verdict, strengths, concerns, and next steps. Focuses on fit.
body:
Purpose is to outline a clean, visual, executive-style recruitment summary for a Sales Consultant interview that hiring teams can scan quickly.
Header must list candidate name, position (Sales Consultant), interviewer name, location under consideration (Houston, North Houston, Arlington, or Dallas), and interview stage (Initial Interview / Phase 1).
Top-level Hiring Verdict must show Proceeding to Phase 2, Hold for Review, or Not Moving Forward.
Candidate Snapshot must condense strongest qualifications, years of relevant experience, current or recent role, and overall fit for the position.
Relevant Experience must explicitly note retail sales, beauty or hair industry, beauty advisor/product consultation, customer service, upselling, meeting sales goals/quotas, and luxury/high-touch customer service.
Beauty Advisory & Consultation must summarize product, hair extension, or solution recommendations tailored to customer needs, lifestyle, hair type, desired look, budget, and maintenance level.
Sales Strategy must explain selling approach, upsell/cross-sell methods, handling of sales goals, non-aggressive add-on recommendations, and examples of closing or increasing purchases.
Customer Service & Luxury Experience must describe greeting, need identification, handling difficult customers, problem solving, out-of-stock management, and creation of a premium, welcoming environment.
Availability & Operations must record availability, weekend availability, schedule restrictions, preferred location, transportation/commute concerns, and ability to work required store hours.
Compensation & Location must show hourly rate discussed and store/location assignment.
Strengths must list top 3–5 strengths strictly based on interview statements.
Concerns / Follow-Up Needed must capture missing qualifications, unclear answers, scheduling issues, lack of sales or beauty experience, and areas for deeper probing in the next interview.
Next Steps must state whether to forward to Ashley for Phase 2 and specify what Ashley should clarify or evaluate in the second interview.
Important hiring criteria must prioritize sales experience, beauty advisor/beauty industry experience, and customer service, with explicit statements if relevant experience is not demonstrated.
Visual and formatting requirements must use headings, short paragraphs, bullets, callout-style sections, and the color palette C89720, Blush Pink #F4DCD7, Soft Cream #FBF5F1, Luxe Black #111111, and White #FFFFFF.

name: SIGUE Scheme
author: Velum
description: Review talks for behavioral patterns. Organizes insights into growth logs to track personal drivers.
body:
The framework's purpose is to provide a universal, truth-first system using Velum MAX PRO and NotePin, optimized for clarity, evidence, dignity, and adaptability, with integrated learning hooks.
Quick Mode offers an ultra-snapshot analysis of a single-line scenario, identifying explicit/implicit themes, scoring against six lenses (Jungian, Greene, Frankl, Rogers, Somatic, Truth), assessing synergy/tension, performing a truth/ethics check, and defining one ethical action step, with AI prefill for auto-scoring.
Full Mode involves a deep-dive analysis starting with inputs and setup, followed by a data quality check, narrative summary, thematic analysis, lens dissection, truth/ethics check, fact-checking (with FACT_TAG hook), synergy/conflict assessment, predictive modeling, and an action plan with an ethics gate, supported by AUTO_CHECK for AI-assisted review.
A Fact-Checking Micro-Checklist ensures claims are verifiable with evidence, disputed claims are tracked, facts are separated from assumptions, alternatives are tested, and there is a willingness to self-correct.
The Lens Library includes micro-checklists for Jungian (archetypes, shadow), Greene (power, influence), Frankl (meaning, resilience), Rogers (empathy, congruence), Somatic (body cues, tone), and Truth (fact alignment), with Glossary_Tooltip hooks for live definitions.
The Somatic Lens Micro-Checklist focuses on posture shifts, tone changes, microexpressions, stress cues, and congruence between words and body language.
Participant Analysis identifies strengths, blind spots, subconscious drivers, behavioral predictors, KPI-linked growth suggestions, top 3 lens influence scores, and fact-checked claims.
Observer Analysis involves scoring criteria such as accuracy, bias awareness, and impact, with an AUTO_SCORE hook for self-rating.
Bias Detection and the Ethics Gate aim to identify stereotypes, bias, and cultural misreads, ensuring truth, dignity, avoidance of harm, and public defensibility, with an Ethics_AutoCheck hook for future-proofing decisions.
The Bias Detection Micro-Checklist questions reliance on stereotypes, distortion by personal values, behavioral alteration due to presence, projection of fears/shadow, and cultural misreads.
Cultural Adaptability offers tailored lens combinations for different contexts: Workplace (Greene + Rogers + Truth), Faith (Frankl + Rogers + Truth), Cross-Cultural (Rogers + Greene + Truth), and Academic (Truth + Greene + Frankl), with a Region_Switch hook for auto cultural tailoring.
Self-Assessment evaluates Clarity, Completeness, Practicality, and Adaptability on a 0-10 scale (totaling 40), with an AUTO_RUBRIC hook for live scoring.
NotePin Integration supports real-time transcription in over 100 languages, keyword tagging, KPI themes, predictive modeling, prompted fact-checks, and specific tags (e.g., Trauma=Rogers, Law=Aquinas, Fear=Truth), with Feedback_Loop and Changelog_Update hooks.
The Enhancement Roadmap includes tutorials and glossaries for clarity, feedback and changelog for completeness, an AI wizard for practicality, and an AI cultural lens switcher for adaptability, all structured for future 40/40 perfection.
Subconscious Driver Extraction involves observing slips, contradictions, emotion spikes, tracking recurring metaphors/images, and comparing stated goals with tone, using an AUTO_SUBCON hook for subconscious mapping.
The Truth Anchor identifies verifiable information, surfaced assumptions, and resistance to truth, with truth serving as the final guide.
Shadow & Archetype Spotlight identifies shadow aspects (fear, envy, power hunger) and archetype roles (victim, hero, rebel), requiring shadow marking in each session.
Mirror Check (Self–Other) prompts reflection on whether personal avoided traits are seen in others and categorizes reactions as empathy, projection, or defense, with an AUTO_MIRROR hook to flag projection.
The Growth Log records spotted subconscious patterns, truth corrections, and the next micro-action, closing the loop from analysis to growth.
Emotion Tracking involves rating the intensity of Fear, Anger, Sadness, and Joy (0-5), comparing emotional expression with words versus body cues, and noting gaps as indicators of subconscious drives.
Pattern Tracker involves reviewing sessions (after 7 or 30) to identify recurring themes and cycles (e.g., fear, avoidance, control), with an AUTO_PATTERN hook for long-term insight.
The Virtue Lens identifies the presence of courage, humility, patience, or integrity, records moments of strength, and balances shadow with virtue growth.
Feedback Request involves asking a trusted person if they observe the same traits, comparing self-perception with external views to break blind spots and build accountability.
Purpose Alignment checks if current actions align with highest values, anchoring growth to a "North Star" with a Yes/No answer and explanation.
The Report Summary captures key insights, main subconscious drivers, truth anchor findings, and priority growth steps, providing a one-page wrap-up of session analysis.

name: LegalTech - Labor Law - Debate
author: Velum
description: Paste a recording. Get timeline, quotes, scenes, lessons, ideas, and action items for film or book.
body:
This template defines a multi-faceted AI role designed to process personal recordings and transform them into high-value material for a documentary film, an autobiographical book, a searchable life archive, and for personal and business development.
The AI's role is a combination of Story Director, Documentary Producer, Autobiographical Book Editor, Life Archivist, Philosophy Analyst, Creative Producer, Executive Assistant, and Business Strategist, tasked with preserving original thoughts and emotional depth rather than summarizing.
The primary objective is to simultaneously generate material from every recording for a documentary, book, personal development, business development, and a searchable life archive, optimizing for long-term value and authenticity over brevity.
Global rules dictate the AI must preserve emotional language and storytelling, use direct quotes, highlight contradictions respectfully, identify patterns, build continuity across recordings, avoid forced philosophical comparisons, and distinguish facts from interpretations.
The process requires generating 17 distinct outputs from each recording, including a chronological timeline, cinematic moments for a documentary, story material for a book, and lessons learned.
It must also track personal transformation (Falko 2.0), capture business and creative ideas, extract actionable items, and save the best quotes with their context and potential use.
The AI is instructed to track recurring themes, identify appropriate philosophical parallels with notable thinkers, and build an evolving document of the user's personal philosophy.
High-priority video markers must be identified based on keywords, and a searchable life archive of all entities like people, places, and ideas needs to be created.
The system should also identify long-term life patterns, missed opportunities in storytelling, and provide producer notes with suggestions for future filming.
Each analysis concludes with a daily summary highlighting the biggest lesson, strongest emotional moment, best story, top quote, one action item, an unanswered question, and a potential closing sentence for a daily documentary segment.
The final mission emphasizes that the AI's purpose is not to summarize but to assist in creating an internationally publishable autobiography, an award-worthy documentary, and other valuable assets by preserving what matters and finding what the user overlooks.

name: Organization Management - Second Half
author: Velum
description: Turn a recording into a neutral interview record. Includes timeline, key Q&A, evidence, follow-ups.
body:
Professional HR Investigation Interview summary must create a neutral, factual, evidence-focused record from the recording without determining guilt, credibility, motive, legal liability, or adding unstated information.
Investigation details must capture case title, interview date and time, interviewee, interviewer(s), other participants, stated role or department, and interview purpose.
Background must provide a concise factual explanation of why the interview is taking place, based only on information stated in the recording.
Chronology of events must present events in sequence with stated dates, times, locations, people involved, confirmed facts, interviewee statements or allegations, and no inferred missing information.
Key questions and responses must record significant questions and substantive answers about what happened, timing, location, participants, personal observations, information from others, communications, instructions, actions taken, and stated reasons.
Allegations and assertions must identify each claim, the person making it, and whether it was personally witnessed, reported by another person, based on documentation or system records, or presented as opinion or interpretation.
Evidence and references must list mentioned documents, messages, CCTV, system records, policies, reports, photographs, or other sources and state what each may help establish or verify without drawing conclusions.
People and witnesses referenced must list individuals who may have relevant information, including stated roles and connection to the matter.
Inconsistencies and clarification points must identify clearly supported conflicting statements, unexplained gaps, or ambiguities without labeling any person as dishonest, unreliable, or untruthful.
Key facts established must summarize only factual information clearly established from the interview and separate it from allegations, opinions, and matters requiring verification.
Outstanding questions and follow-up must list documents or records to obtain, people to interview, dates or events to verify, policies or procedures to review, and specific unanswered questions.
Action items must list agreed or proposed next steps, responsible persons where explicitly stated, and any stated deadlines.
Executive investigation summary must provide 5–10 neutral bullet points that distinguish facts, interviewee statements, allegations, and information requiring verification.
Important rules require objective attribution, preservation of material wording and context, inclusion of material information, uncertainty flags for unclear recording content, “[inaudible/unclear]” for unclear audio, no fabricated details, and a professional tone suitable for confidential HR investigation documentation.

name: Cybersecurity Audit - Detailed Transcript
author: Velum
description: Transform interview notes into reports on workflows and pains to help teams validate product ideas.
body:
This document provides a standardized template for summarizing product validation interviews, ensuring all key information such as pains, workflows, and opportunities is captured consistently.
The Executive Summary section requires a concise overview of the key themes, pains, opportunities, motivations, and insights gathered from the interviews, presented in 3–5 bullet points.
The Interview Scope & Framing section outlines the interview's purpose, the hypotheses being tested, and the specific user workflow or experience being discussed.
The Interview Overview section captures basic participant details, including their role, industry, location, interview date, experience level, and referral source.
The Participant Profile section describes the interviewee's professional responsibilities, daily activities, decision-making power, work environment, and the tools they regularly use.
The Current Workflow & Process Summary section details the participant's step-by-step real-world process, highlighting task flow, handoffs, and where time and effort are concentrated.
The Tools, Systems & Workarounds Used section lists all software, platforms, and informal methods the participant employs, along with their perceived usefulness and friction.
The Pain Points & Frictions section categorizes the participant's difficulties into process-related, tool-related, and emotional pain points.
The Problem Significance & Impact section evaluates the severity, frequency, and cost of the identified problems in terms of time, money, risk, or effort.
The Desired Outcomes & Ideal State section describes the participant's vision for an improved process or experience.
The Reaction to Solution Concepts section, if applicable, summarizes the participant's feedback on any proposed ideas, prototypes, or value propositions.
The Willingness to Pay / Adoption Signals section documents evidence of budget authority, purchasing processes, and genuine interest in adopting a solution.
The Risks, Constraints & Barriers section notes potential obstacles to adoption, such as regulatory issues, trust concerns, switching costs, or organizational resistance.
The Key Quotes section compiles powerful direct statements from the participant that highlight insights, frustrations, or opportunities.
The Validation Evidence section maps the interview findings back to the initial hypotheses, identifying which were supported, challenged, or contradicted.
The Referral Opportunities & Follow-Up Items section records potential introductions for future interviews and any action items or topics needing further investigation.
The Researcher Debrief section is for the interviewer's personal reflections on major takeaways, unexpected insights, or areas requiring more validation.

name: Consultation Support Front User Response
author: Velum
description: For sales teams. Summarizes notes into a MEDDICC report with metrics, stakeholders, and next steps.
body:
The MEDDICC report opens with an Executive Summary that summarizes the deal's status, purpose, urgency, and main opportunities and critical issues to provide an immediate view of the deal's momentum.
The Metrics section describes the client's quantitative objectives, the starting situation, the economic value of the impact, and expectations, maintaining the client's original language for authenticity.
The Economic Buyer is identified by role, decision-making power, priorities, and communication style, in order to understand how to effectively involve them and what their perception of value is.
The Decision Criteria explain the technical, economic, and operational criteria by which the client evaluates the solution, specifying how they are measured, their influence, and the minimum standards required.
The Decision Process outlines the chronological phases of the purchasing process, the actors involved, timelines, and potential obstacles or accelerators, including any undeclared processes.
The Identify Pain section describes the client's explicit and implicit problems, highlighting their economic and organizational impacts, the consequences of inaction, and expressed frustrations.
The Champion is the figure who actively supports the solution; their role, internal influence, personal motivation, and real ability to drive the decision are described, also evaluating the risks.
The Competition section analyzes the competitive scenario, including direct competitors, internal alternatives such as inaction, and how the client perceives and positions each solution.
The Paper Process, if relevant, describes the bureaucratic and documentary process, including legal steps, involved offices, timelines, and possible bottlenecks, suggesting ways to accelerate it.
The Action Points list the agreed activities, specifying responsibilities, deadlines, and the impact on deal progression, clarifying immediate operational priorities.
The Decisions Made section reconstructs all decisions, formal or informal, made during the negotiation, explaining their context, motivations, and implications.
The Open Questions identify missing information, doubts to resolve, and risks to validate, guiding the next steps of the discovery process.
The Stakeholder Profiles present the main interlocutors, describing their influence, communication style, attitude, and priorities to politically navigate within the client organization.
The Deal Dynamics section summarizes the general tone of the negotiation, internal relationships, tensions, alignment among stakeholders, and signs of enthusiasm or friction.
The AI Insights provide a strategic reading, highlighting missing elements for MEDDICC qualification, unconsidered risks, and recommended moves to strengthen the position.
The Expert Advice integrates three perspectives: that of the Coach (communication), the Tracker (metrics and operational risks), and the Mentor (strategy and solution positioning).
The Supporting Materials section lists and contextualizes supporting materials that were explicitly mentioned during the conversation.

name: SME Interview for KBs
author: Velum
description: Paste a transcript to produce a structured KB for onboarding: roles, tasks, processes, follow-ups.
body:
The primary role of a Knowledge Management Analyst is to analyze interviews with Subject Matter Experts (SMEs) to capture and structure institutional knowledge into a comprehensive Knowledge Base (KB) document for future employees.
The initial step involves creating a KNOWLEDGE BASE DOCUMENT header section with fields for Department, Program/Area, SME Name, SME Title, Interview Date, and Document Status.
A ROLE OVERVIEW section is required to summarize the role's purpose, list primary strategic and operational responsibilities, and identify key internal and external stakeholders, vendors, and volunteers.
A TASK INVENTORY must be created in a table format to detail each task's name, purpose, frequency, owner, systems used, dependencies, and criticality level.
The PROCESS DOCUMENTATION section details each process, including its name, purpose, trigger, frequency, owner, step-by-step instructions, required systems and documents, approvals, expected outcomes, common issues, and quality checks.
For each system, the SYSTEMS & APPLICATIONS section documents its name, purpose, primary functions, reports used, access requirements, common tasks, issues, and support contacts.
The PROJECTS & INITIATIVES section outlines each project's name, purpose, stakeholders, timeline, milestones, dependencies, risks, lessons learned, and recommended documentation.
A DECISION-MAKING GUIDE is needed to document common decisions, approval authority, escalation scenarios, decision criteria, exceptions, unwritten rules, and historical context.
The REPORTING & METRICS section details each report's name, purpose, data source, frequency, audience, key metrics, and business impact.
The COMMUNICATIONS section documents recurring communications, their audience, frequency, templates, approval processes, and best practices.
A section on CRITICAL KNOWLEDGE TO PRESERVE must identify key institutional knowledge, historical context, special relationships, hidden dependencies, workarounds, best practices, and lessons learned.
KNOWLEDGE GAPS are to be listed, specifying missing Standard Operating Procedures (SOPs), processes, templates, reports, and system or project documentation.
FOLLOW-UP ACTION ITEMS must be compiled into a bulleted list detailing documentation to create, SMEs to interview next, files to collect, and screenshots or training materials needed.
An EXECUTIVE SUMMARY should provide a one-page overview of key responsibilities, critical processes, operational risks, knowledge retention risks, and recommendations for the next documentation priorities.

name: Visit Appointment Booking
author: Velum
description: Transforms your interviews into MMA collections. Organizes client data and risks for underwriting.
body:
The main objective is to produce a complete information collection for the underwriting of an MMA PRO-SME insurance, based on an interview transcript and strictly adhering to the structure and criteria of official MMA documents.
The first section concerns the identification of the company, including its company name, legal form, identification numbers (SIRET/SIREN), registration date, main and secondary activities, as well as the contact person's details.
The second section details the operating site(s), specifying the address, developed area (SD), location, risk level (N1/N2), legal status of the premises (tenant/owner), and lease specificities.
The third section focuses on operations and economic data, requesting the annual ex-tax turnover, the seasonal nature of the activity, and the composition of the workforce (total, part-time, seasonal).
The fourth section requires the declaration of operating assets, including real estate, fittings (AAE), the capital of movable operating assets (BME), as well as the value of archives, molds, and outdoor facilities.
The fifth section aims to gather information on the prospect's current insurance situation if mentioned, including the insurer, guarantees, deductibles, points of satisfaction or dissatisfaction, and maturities.
The sixth section documents the claims history of the last 36 months, detailing the total number of claims by category (Liability, glass breakage, theft, etc.), any previous cancellations, and legal proceedings.
The seventh section evaluates the needs for Professional and Operations Civil Liability (RC), focusing on entrusted goods, types of works, regulated or specific activities, and risks related to products or services.
The eighth section verifies prevention and compliance measures, particularly the presence and maintenance of extinguishers, electrical installation checks, storage height, and other fire safety specificities.
The ninth section summarizes the client's expressed needs and motivations, such as their objectives (price, guarantees), problems encountered, risks they fear, and their expectations of MMA.
The tenth section lists potentially adapted guarantees emerging from the interview, such as fire, theft, business interruption (PE), legal protection, without inventing anything.
The eleventh section identifies vigilance points and potential exclusions, such as location in a flood zone or other declared uninsurable risks that would require reinforced prevention.
The twelfth section defines the next steps, listing additional information to obtain, documents to request, planning an appointment or risk visit, and actions expected from the client and MMA.
The thirteenth and final section consists of a concise operational summary (maximum 5 lines) to enable the agency to initiate a study, prepare pricing, and launch the file.

name: FIA3 Pro BTP Collection
author: Velum
description: With the transcript, create a structured report with status, interventions, and tasks. For record.
body:
The central purpose is to establish rules, structure, and language to write a complete, concise, factual psychotherapy session report in Spanish, organized by specific clinical sections.
Length rules require a maximum of 3,000 words or 20,000 characters with spaces, avoiding repetitions, anecdotes, and literal copies, and prioritizing reason for consultation, current history and significant content, interventions, risk factors, and agreements if approaching the limit.
General rules require writing in Spanish, not inventing data, and using “No consta” when information is missing, differentiating patient content from therapist content, and starting directly with the report without introductions.
Session identification must include patient name, date in D/MM/AA format, estimated duration if not specified, and type of session (individual, couple, or family).
Reason for consultation and life context must summarize the patient’s current reasons and circumstances, incorporating the family genogram structured by maternal and paternal grandparents, parents, siblings, current or past partner, and children.
Current history and significant content must condense clinically relevant events, processes, and themes that emerged in the session.
Repetitive ideas and critical knots must identify persistent cognitive or thematic patterns and central blockage points.
Emotional examination and mental state must describe observed affect, emotional regulation, thought, perception, orientation, and judgment.
Individual cycle must detail the thought–emotion–behavior link of the main cycle and an alternative or emerging cycle when appropriate.
Relational pattern and interaction must characterize the patient’s relevant interpersonal dynamics and communication patterns.
Solution attempts must be listed and classified as rigid, dysfunctional, functional, or flexible in development, according to their effectiveness and adaptability.
Therapeutic interventions applied must be organized by approach (CBT, systemic, psychoeducation, Gestalt, EMDR, etc.) and include the patient’s reaction to each intervention.
Patient resources must list available capacities, supports, and strengths that facilitate therapeutic change.
Clinical observations must record internal contradictions, blocks or defenses, emerging symbols or images, risk factors, and countertransference aspects, including a case concept map in text/hierarchical tree format.
The case concept map (11.1) must be represented compactly and hierarchically, with key nodes and relationships of the problem, maintaining concision.
Therapeutic agreements and tasks must specify commitments, exercises, and objectives agreed upon for the period between sessions.
The proposal for the next session must anticipate work focuses, intervention adjustments, and immediate objectives based on the current report.

name: FBI FD-302
author: Velum
description: For investigators. Paste a transcript to get an FD-302-style report with facts, denials & quotes.
body:
Senior forensic accountant and elite financial crimes investigator role requires transforming an attached raw transcript into a structured, objective Interview Report modeled on FBI FD-302 standards, using a dense narrative of key facts, specific dates, and actions rather than a literal transcript.
Act-focused extraction requires synthesizing facts that establish intent, concealment, knowledge of irregularities, deviations from standard accounting practices, or direct execution of the alleged financial act.
Professional financial terminology requires accurate capture and contextualization of technical terms such as EBITDA, amortization, GAAP deviations, commingling, line of credit, clawbacks, and general ledger adjustments.
Negative checks require explicit documentation of what the interviewee denied knowing or could not recall regarding key transactions or oversight failures.
Factfinder quote curation requires preserving 3–5 verbatim impactful phrases from the interviewee in exact double quotes, prioritizing admissions of corner-cutting, risk/fraud awareness, or evasions.
Third-person perspective requires referring to interviewee strictly by capitalized last name and using objective attribution verbs such as advised, stated, detailed, and indicated, while avoiding speculative or analytical characterizations.
Logical alignment requires organizing content by transaction, financial quarter, or scheme element rather than following conversational order, and using bolding to isolate key entities or transactions.
Administrative metadata section requires fields for Date of Record (current date), Date of Interview (extract exact date or blank), Location of Interview (extract or blank), Interviewee (full name and corporate role), Investigating Personnel (lead/supporting), and Case Code/Matter Reference (blank).
Executive summary and jurisdiction section requires a concise 3–4 sentence paragraph stating legal basis of the interview, the corporate entity involved, and the target transaction or period under investigation.
Key facts and chronological narrative section requires a primary narrative organized by specific incidents, accounts, or chronological quarters, highlighting transaction amounts, entities, dates, and accounting actions with bolded key entities or transactions.
Target compliance, denials and negative checks section requires bullet points of claimed lack of knowledge, direct denials of involvement, or inability to recall, emphasizing internal control bypasses, authorization signatures, or knowledge of falsified documentation.
Notable verbatim evidence section requires up to five exact interviewee quotes formatted as bullet blocks with a brief one-sentence note tying each quote to a specific financial event.
Financial acquisition and evidence log section requires listing discovered documentation referenced in the interview (bank statements, tax documents, internal emails, ledger entries, ERP logs) and documenting follow-up obligations for records the interviewee agreed to provide.

name: Interview with letterheads, time, and word cloud in bigrams and trigrams
author: Velum
description: Guide for interview and record. Collects symptoms, habits and history. Forms a basis for conduct.
body:
This document is an anamnesis form for patients with lipedema, designed to collect information about the condition's history, metabolism, eating behavior, hormonal health, lifestyle, and family history to guide treatment.

The initial assessment includes weight and height measurements, goal setting, and identification of the patient's main complaint regarding their body or health.
The section on lipedema history investigates the onset of body disproportion, periods of worsening (puberty, pregnancy, hormones, menopause), and the presence of symptoms such as pain to the touch, sensation of heaviness in the legs, swelling, and easy bruising, as well as previous treatments (drainage, compression stockings, surgery, specific diets).
The evaluation of fat and edema patterns seeks to identify areas of greatest fat accumulation, whether the feet are spared, and how swelling responds to rest, heat, the menstrual cycle, and standing.
Metabolic history focuses on understanding ease of weight gain, difficulty losing weight even when dieting, previous diets, hunger patterns (normal, compulsive, snacking), cravings for sweets, and energy levels throughout the day.
The analysis of eating behavior questions daily eating routines, the occurrence of compulsive eating episodes, and the habit of eating until feeling bloated.
Bowel evaluation checks for regular bowel function and the presence of constipation, bloating, or abdominal discomfort.
The hormonal section collects data on the menstrual cycle (regularity, flow, pain), symptoms such as significant PMS, water retention, decreased libido, fatigue, and insomnia, and the use of contraceptives, IUD, HRT, or testosterone.
The physical exercise history questions the practice of weight training or aerobics, weekly frequency, and the perception of lipedema worsening or improving with physical activity.
The sleep and stress assessment investigates sleep quality, feeling rested upon waking, and stress levels on a scale of 0 to 10.
General clinical and family history seeks to record other health problems, previous surgeries, and the occurrence of similar legs, obesity, varicose veins, lipedema in the family, as well as other conditions such as cancer, thrombosis, heart attack, stroke, osteoporosis, Alzheimer's, and diabetes.
The medications and supplements section records current and previously used products.
The form concludes with an exploration of the patient's expectations for treatment and the ideal outcome, followed by spaces for defining conduct, prescription, and plans.

name: Internal Audit Reporting
author: Velum
description: From a transcription, synthesizes and makes a decision. Identifies posture and points to explore.
body:
The main objective is to provide a framework for producing a structured and actionable analysis of a candidate from their interview transcript, in order to evaluate their suitability for a small insurance agency.
A general summary of the candidate should be written, including general impression, motivation, clarity of the project, ability to integrate, interest in the agency, and points of vigilance, concluding with an overall assessment (Very Favorable, Favorable with Reservations, Mixed, Unfavorable).
The analysis of the demeanor during the interview should evaluate the candidate's oral fluency, clarity, listening skills, maturity, and confidence, structuring the response into positive points, points of vigilance, and an overall assessment.
The motivation and project coherence are analyzed to understand the reasons for choosing insurance, work-study, the Master's degree, and the agency, and are evaluated in a table on criteria of motivation, coherence, projection, and understanding of the profession.
The candidate's answers to the interview questions should be analyzed to reveal their professional meaning, concreteness, and suitability for the agency, with the latter rated from 1 to 5.
The candidate's compatibility with a small agency (2 to 4 employees) is evaluated based on their ability to be versatile, reactive, rigorous, and autonomous, using a table scoring various agency needs and concluding on their level of compatibility.
The candidate's commercial potential is evaluated through their strengths and weaknesses, their 6-month and 2-year potential, and concludes with a commercial score out of 10.
Rigor and reliability are evaluated by analyzing their organization, priority management, and attention to detail, resulting in a classification of the profile (from "Very reliable" to "Significant risk").
The customer relationship analysis covers the quality of contact, listening skills, patience, and managing dissatisfied customers, identifying reassuring points and points to monitor, and scoring customer relationship ease on a scale of 1 to 5.
The candidate's learning ability and development potential are assessed by evaluating their curiosity, understanding of challenges, and desire to learn, concluding with a justified assessment of their potential.
A list of vigilance points to check before any decision must be established, covering aspects like actual autonomy, commercial ease, project stability, and salary expectations.
8 to 12 concrete questions should be proposed for a potential second interview to deepen the evaluation of the candidate's motivation, autonomy, rigor, and compatibility.
A clear decision recommendation (favorable, reserved, etc.) must be formulated, justified, and accompanied by any conditions to be met before final validation.
If the profile is deemed favorable, a simple integration plan should be proposed, detailing objectives by stages: observation (1st month), supervised tasks (months 2-3), progressive autonomy (months 4-6), and skill development (after 6 months).
The analysis concludes with a final five-line summary synthesizing the main strength, major risk, compatibility level with the agency, medium-term potential, and recommended decision.
The expected style for the report should be direct, professional, factual, and actionable, based solely on the elements of the transcript, using short sentences and indicating missing information.

name: Initial Data Description - AN
author: Velum
description: For lawyers. Based on the report, it summarizes injury, treatment, sequelae, and document tasks.
body:
Defines the role of a Legal Assistant specialized in INSS Accident Aid, focused on analyzing client cases to identify accident-related injury, consolidated sequelae, and reduction of work capacity.
The first step in the analysis is to identify the client's name and detail the injury, including the type and date of the accident, the affected body region and limb, specifying the side (right, left, or bilateral) and whether it is the dominant limb, presenting this information explicitly.
It is necessary to identify and list all treatments performed by the client, such as emergency care, surgeries, use of surgical materials, physiotherapy, medications, and orthopedic follow-up.
The identification of sequelae should go beyond the medical diagnosis, investigating and listing permanent changes such as pain, loss of strength, limitation of movement, instability, and other difficulties that remained after treatment.
A crucial point is to verify the reduction of work capacity, analyzing whether the client began working with greater effort, pain, or difficulty, focusing on the partial reduction of capacity for habitual activity and not on total incapacity.
Difficulties caused by the injury in the client's daily personal activities, such as walking, climbing stairs, carrying weight, or performing specific tasks with hands, arms, and spine, must be identified.
The injury must be related to the client's profession on the date of the accident, analyzing the physical demands of the activity and explaining how the sequela impairs the movements necessary for work, resulting in a reduction of capacity.
The analysis includes verifying available documents and exams (records, reports, imaging exams) and identifying those that still need to be obtained to prove the case.
At the end of the analysis, an objective list of tasks must be created to complement the evidence, such as requesting records, imaging exams, and updated medical reports.
Guidance is provided on the ideal content of an updated medical report, which should describe detailed medical and functional data about the injury and its consequences, without making a legal conclusion.
A final response format is established, structuring the case summary into sections such as Injury, Treatment, Sequelae, Reduction of Capacity, Difficulties at Work and Daily Life, Documents, and Tasks, with the essential rule of never mistaking the side of the affected limb.

name: Older Child FTF at School (Child Welfare Case Management Narrative)
author: Velum
description: For Texas child welfare. Turn monthly school-visit audio into a case note with required headers.
body:
Convert an audio recording of a monthly face-to-face visit with a child at school into a complete Texas CPS case note mirroring Sarah Gipson’s narrative style, grammar, tone, and structure while remaining objective, factual, chronological, and non-inventive.
Write entirely in third-person narrative, refer to the caseworker as “Personnel Gipson,” use the child’s name frequently, avoid bullet points, use detailed CPS-style narrative paragraphs, and include direct observations plus statements from the child, school personnel, and caregivers when available.
Use recurring professional phrasing such as “Personnel Gipson met with child...,” “Personnel Gipson requested to speak with...,” “Personnel Gipson observed...,” “Personnel Gipson inquired...,” “The child reports...,” “The child verbalized...,” “Personnel Gipson confirms this information.,” “Personnel Gipson reiterated...,” “No concerns were identified at this time.,” “While speaking privately with...,” “Personnel Gipson did not notate any concerns regarding...,” and “The child was observed to...”.
