Format the document with the specified headers for MONTHLY REQUIRED FTF CONTACT WITH CHILDREN, including CONTACTED BY, DATE, TIME, ESTIMATED TIME WITH CLIENT, PURPOSE (CVS MONTHLY REQUIRED (FTF)), METHOD (FACE TO FACE), ANNOUNCED OR UNANNOUNCED, LOCATION, OTHERS CONTACTED, and PRINCIPALS/COLLATERALS CONTACTED.
Provide an INITIAL SCHOOL CONTACT NARRATIVE covering school name and location, announced versus unannounced visit, arrival process, personnel contacted, access procedures to the child, staff interactions, identification/sign-in procedures, who was present, privacy status, and observations of clothing, grooming, hygiene, mood, affect, injuries/marks, and behavior during the meeting.
Document FAMILY CONTACT/VISITATION details including parent and sibling visitation schedules, feelings about visits, phone/virtual contact, supervision level, relationships with parents and siblings, requested changes, upcoming visits, and emotional impact.
Document PLACEMENT/SAFETY details including current placement and household composition, adjustment, relationships within the home, feelings about placement, sense of safety, rules and discipline, sleeping arrangements, whether needs are met, supervision concerns, identified safety concerns, and placement stability assessment.
Document EDUCATIONAL NEEDS details including current school, grade, attendance, performance, favorite/least favorite subjects, teacher relationships, behavioral/disciplinary issues, special education services, IEP, ARD meetings, 504 accommodations, activities, goals/interests, staff feedback when available, and identified educational needs.
Document PERMANENCY GOAL/CASE STATUS details including primary and concurrent permanency goals, child’s understanding of the case, reunification efforts, relative or fictive kin options, court updates, service plan progress, child’s wishes, additional services needed, and upcoming hearings/meetings/events.
Document ADJUSTMENT/WELL-BEING details including understanding of being in care, feelings about placement, emotional and behavioral functioning, strengths, coping skills, accomplishments, self-esteem, peer relationships, overall adjustment, concerns, and outlook/future goals.
Document MEDICAL/DENTAL NEEDS details including overall health, illnesses, injuries, medications, medical and dental appointments, sleep, appetite, physical observations, hygiene, and pending evaluations or treatment.
Document THERAPEUTIC NEEDS/SERVICES details including counseling participation, therapist information, service frequency, child’s perception of counseling, psychiatric services, psychological evaluations, referrals, compliance, progress, and recommendations/next steps.
Document SOCIAL/EMOTIONAL NEEDS details including friendships, peer interactions, extracurricular activities, hobbies, sports, community involvement, church involvement if mentioned, recreational interests, social opportunities, emotional supports, and positive activities.
Address TRANSITIONAL PLANNING for children age 16+ including PAL participation, employment, driver’s license, transportation needs, educational/college/vocational planning, housing goals, independent living skills, adult support systems, life skills development, and transition readiness, and state “Transitional planning is not applicable due to the child’s age.” when the child is under age 16.
Provide a CASEWORKER ASSESSMENT narrative summarizing educational functioning, placement stability, physical health, emotional well-being, therapeutic participation, safety assessment, permanency progress, child strengths, identified concerns, and follow-up actions needed.
Conclude with ENDING DOCUMENTATION LANGUAGE in Sarah Gipson’s style including whether a photo was obtained if mentioned, follow-up completed, how the contact ended, whether the child returned to class, information received from school staff, and future action items.
State “Not discussed during this monthly contact.” for any required topic that was not discussed.

name: Student Interview Summary Sheet
author: Velum
description: Organize data from the mill visit. Produce a report with indicators, debt, and payment capacity.
body:
The objective is to provide a structured model for preparing a credit risk visit and analysis report for sugar and ethanol mills, focusing on technical indicators and payment capacity.
The Identification section requires collecting basic information about the company, such as name, economic group, location, date of visit, participants, harvest analyzed, and legal status.
The Executive Summary should synthesize in up to 10 lines the economic-financial situation, operational capacity, agricultural condition, efficiency, profitability, indebtedness, risks, mitigators, and a preliminary conclusion on payment capacity.
The Operational Profile focuses on presenting data on milling capacity (nominal and effective), utilization, production mix (sugar/ethanol), total production, and any industrial bottlenecks.
The Agricultural Performance analysis should be done in a table comparing indicators such as TCH, ATR, TAH, age of sugarcane fields, and costs with previous harvests and benchmarks, as well as evaluating the causes of any deterioration.
Industrial Performance uses a table to evaluate indicators such as capacity utilization, efficiency, losses, and industrial yields compared to benchmarks, also identifying bottlenecks and maintenance needs.
The Costs, Margins and Competitiveness section aims to present financial data such as net revenue, EBITDA, margins, and costs, comparing them with industry references to assess the mill's competitiveness.
CAPEX analysis should detail investments (agricultural and industrial) made and planned, separating them by category (maintenance, expansion) and assessing whether there are repressed investments impacting the operation.
The evaluation of Working Capital and Harvest Financing aims to identify cash needs, financing sources (CPR, ACC/ACE, banks), guarantees, and liquidity risk during the off-season period.
The Commercialization and Hedge section should present the percentage of production with fixed prices, hedge policies for commodities and exchange rates, and the company's overall exposure to market fluctuations.
Indebtedness analysis requires creating a table with the debt profile (balance, cost, maturity, guarantees) and calculating leverage indicators such as Net Debt/EBITDA.
For companies in Judicial Recovery, it is necessary to detail the plan conditions, such as credit value, haircut, deadlines, and assess whether operational cash generation supports the restructured debt service.
The Cash Flow and Payment Capacity section structures the calculation of free cash flow (FCF) from EBITDA and calculates the debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) to classify payment risk.
Main Risks should be listed objectively, relating them to the observed numerical indicators, such as low agricultural productivity, repressed capex, high leverage, or liquidity pressure.
Mitigators identify strengths that can counterbalance risks, such as asset quality, owned land, hedge, firm contracts, or the entry of a strategic investor.
The Credit Conclusion should objectively answer whether the operation is economically viable, classify the operational situation, and conclude by evaluating whether the mill has the capacity to generate FCF to maintain its assets and service the restructured debt.
A final diagnostic chart is suggested to classify the main pillars of the analysis with a color system (green, yellow, red): Agricultural, Industrial, Competitiveness, Investments, Cash, Indebtedness, and Judicial Recovery.

name: SUPERVISION MHD
author: Velum
description: From a transcription, fill out the factual MMA Auto Fleet collection. "Not specified" if absent.
body:
The main objective is to create a structured information collection for an MMA car fleet insurance contract, based on a transcription, strictly complying with MMA models, general conditions, and the Insurance Code.
The first section aims to collect basic company identification information, including its name, address, creation date, NAF code, SIRET number, and number of employees.
The company's legal and financial situation is assessed, including the existence of collective procedures, knowledge of the fleet budget, current maturity, and desired contract takeover date.
Desired contract management methods are defined, including the management mode (per movement, periodical, by half-difference), contribution fractionation, and any applicable MMA commercial campaign.
It is necessary to identify specific risk activities, such as the transport of hazardous materials (ADR) or circulation on airport runways, which may require an additional questionnaire.
The structure of the car fleet must be detailed by vehicle category (VP, LCV, TRUCKS, TRAILERS, 2-wheelers, machinery, etc.) to understand the evolution and total number of vehicles to be insured.
The analysis of claims history over the last four exercises is a major criterion, requiring details of claims by nature, cost, and responsibility, with particular attention to major claims (RC > €30,000, Damages > €25,000).
Current guarantees of the ongoing contract, such as Motor Liability, Glass Breakage, or All Risks Damage, must be listed for each vehicle category.
The current deductibles applied by guarantee and by vehicle category, as well as the declared insured value, must be specified.
Client-desired modifications to their current contract, whether adding, strengthening, or removing guarantees, or changing deductibles, must be clearly expressed.
Specific options and extensions requested, such as Compensation +, professional fittings guarantee, or coverage for high-end vehicles (> €80,000), are to be listed.
Information on existing assistance must be collected, including formulas subscribed by category, 0 km breakdown option, and provision of a replacement vehicle.
Contractual vigilance points, such as uninsurable vehicles, public transport, rental without driver, or novice drivers, must be identified.
Actions to be taken by the MMA agency are defined, including obtaining information statements, the need for an additional questionnaire, and steps leading to the admissibility decision.
A concise operational summary must be written to allow for a quick decision by the underwriting department or the General Agent, strictly adhering to contractual and factual vocabulary.

name: ANNUAL INTERVIEW FOR HEALTHCARE EXECUTIVE
author: Velum
description: Generates competency and culture reports based on transcriptions to support selection decisions.
body:
The main objective is to provide a detailed model for conducting and analyzing job interviews with multiple evaluators, focusing on faithful transcription, evaluation of behavioral competencies, and the candidate's cultural alignment with the company.
The first step is to contextualize the interview, recording the candidate's name, role, date, and evaluators present.
It is necessary to perform a literal transcription of the interview audio, separating speeches by speaker (Speaker 1, Speaker 2, etc.) and maintaining timestamp formatting, without corrections or interpretations.
The speaking time of each participant should be calculated and analyzed to determine if the communication was dominated by the candidate, balanced, or if the candidate was withdrawn, in addition to noting the frequency of interruptions.
The candidate's active listening is evaluated based on their ability to listen to the end, answer what was asked, frequency of interruptions, and emotional presence, concluding whether it is adequate to the required level.
Speech coherence is analyzed from logical, emotional, temporal, and value perspectives, checking narrative consistency, especially under pressure, and identifying signs of rehearsed or evasive speeches.
The CSTAR model is used to evaluate the candidate's character (integrity, ethics), reliability (transparency, admission of errors), and loyalty (stability, long-term vision).
Alignment with company culture is measured through criteria such as sense of urgency, pace, communication, resilience, openness to feedback, and congruence between discourse and attitude.
Readiness for immediate results is evaluated considering mental agility, objectivity, autonomy, stability under challenge, and decision-making capacity, to verify if it meets the company's current needs.
Emotional maturity is examined by stability, reaction to confrontations, emotional control, tone of voice, self-criticism, and self-awareness, to determine if it is adequate to the required level.
Growth potential is assessed by learning ability, ego flexibility, perceived evolution during the interview, structured ambition, depth of answers, and tolerance to complexity, concluding on the possibility of internal development.
It is necessary to describe the tone of voice and emotional states manifested by the candidate, such as nervousness, confidence, defensiveness, or insecurity, observing variations in energy and discomfort.
Any contradictions in the candidate's answers should be identified and documented, comparing divergent speech excerpts and interpreting them as omission, incoherence, or narrative instability.
It is necessary to objectively list the strengths and warning signs or risks identified in the candidate, covering emotional, cultural, coherence, and behavioral aspects.
Agreements, such as expectations, commitments, and next steps defined at the end of the interview, should be recorded.
The unified closing consolidates the evaluation with an Overall Rating based on all previous metrics and a final decisive verdict, such as "Highly Reliable and Aligned" or "Not Recommended".

name: Appointment 2 BC
author: Velum
description: Structures crisis and finance data in reports. Assists in the preparation of judicial requests.
body:
The main objective is to act as a legal assistant to automatically generate a structured interview report, which will serve as the basis for preparing a Judicial Recovery request.
The report should begin with the complete identification of the company, including its corporate name, CNPJ, address, business sector, CNAE, corporate structure, shareholder participation, and the existence of branches or other companies within the same economic group.
It is necessary to detail the history of the crisis, specifying its beginning, the main causes (such as revenue drop, debts, or mismanagement), its nature (operational, financial, etc.), and the future prospects of the business.
The current financial situation must be documented, covering revenue for the last 24 months, cash flow, categorized debts (banking, suppliers, labor, tax), and the existence of protests, judicial executions, or blockages.
The company's assets and guarantees, such as machinery, real estate, and brands, should be listed, identifying which are essential, which can be sold, and if partners' assets have been given as collateral.
Accounting analysis requires financial statements for the last 3 years, updated Income Statement (DRE) and balance sheets, information on accounting organization, external audits, and inventory control and accounts receivable.
Information on human resources needs to be gathered, including the number of employees, overdue amounts (salaries, FGTS), ongoing labor lawsuits, and the risk of mass layoffs.
The evaluation of essential contracts and operations involves identifying key contracts, critical suppliers, insolvency termination clauses, and immediate risks to business continuity.
Tax liabilities must be detailed, including tax debts at all levels (federal, state, municipal), current installment plans, and enrollments in active debt.
The legal history of the company and its partners needs to be verified, including previous recovery requests, bankruptcies declared in the group, or criminal investigations.
It is fundamental to define the objectives of the Judicial Recovery request, such as debt renegotiation or suspension of executions, and to assess the company's ability to maintain operations and willingness for documentary transparency.
Finally, a list of documents required for analysis by the office should be provided, such as balance sheets, creditor and asset lists, bank statements, certificates, employee lists, and relevant contracts.

name: Child Interviews
author: Velum
description: Structure interview notes into reports. Captures well-being and safety to assist documentation.
body:
The primary purpose is to provide a structured format for transcribing and summarizing interviews with children in high-conflict custody cases for a Florida Guardian ad Litem report, ensuring the child's perspective is captured neutrally and accurately.
The initial step involves identifying the child's name, age, grade, who brought them to the interview, the setting, and their initial demeanor.
The child's general well-being should be assessed by documenting their emotional state, physical health, school performance, friendships, activities, and personal strengths.
For both the mother's and father's households, the summary must capture daily routines, the child's sense of safety, described rules and discipline, the emotional climate, family dynamics, and any specific positive or negative statements made by the child.
The report must detail the child's specific concerns, including any fears, worries, or mentions of conflict, violence, substance use, instability, neglect, pressure, or loyalty conflicts.
The child's stated preferences regarding custody and time-sharing must be recorded, including where they want to live, their preferred schedule, and the reasons for their preferences, while also noting any signs of coaching.
The child's perspective on each parent should be summarized, covering their views on parenting strengths and weaknesses, fairness, reliability, communication, conflict handling, and any unmet needs.
Sibling dynamics should be documented, including how they get along, whether conflict varies between households, and any concerns the child has for their siblings' well-being.
The summary should include information on the child's support systems, such as teachers or relatives, the importance of stability, and their thoughts on potential major life changes like moving or new partners.
Any statements from the child indicating imminent risk or requiring mandatory reporting must be captured under safety statements, along with any retracted or hesitant disclosures.
The report must flag potential indicators of coaching or undue influence, such as rehearsed phrases, changes in tone, age-inappropriate knowledge, or emotional dysregulation linked to one parent.
A final narrative summary from the child's point of view should be provided in a neutral, third-person form, highlighting what is most important to the child, their fears, and what they want the court to understand about the family conflict.
The Guardian ad Litem's observational notes, which are not attributed to the child, should document the child's affect, body language, regulation level, and any concerns about the reliability of their statements or need for follow-up.
The summary concludes by stating it is the child's account unless noted otherwise and is followed by an interview analysis with follow-up questions and tasks for the child.

name: Aptitude & Reasoning Evaluation
author: Velum
description: Verbatim, timestamped transcript with speaker labels, plus a neutral summary and question-style review.
body:
The primary objective is to transcribe and summarize recorded child forensic interviews into a neutral, court-ready document.
The process begins with creating a verbatim transcription, distinguishing between the interviewer and child, including timestamps, and marking inaudible sections, without paraphrasing substantive content or removing filler words.
Following transcription, a detailed summary analyzes the interview's structure, assessing phases like rapport building, ground rules discussion, practice narrative, and the substantive phase, focusing on adherence to best-practice forensic protocols.
The analysis includes commentary on deviations from structured models, such as leading or suggestive questioning, and notes on the child's memory, like expressions of "I don't know" or "I don't remember."
Interviewer prompts are categorized into types: open-ended invitations, cued invitations, direct questions, option-posing questions, and suggestive/leading questions.
Summary metrics are calculated, including the percentage of open-ended, directive, and leading questions, along with the percentage of words spoken by the interviewer versus the child.
The analysis comments on how questioning style might influence the reliability of information, and whether alternative hypotheses were explored.
Child response characteristics are evaluated for narrative coherence, level of detail, spontaneity, consistency, and the use of child-like versus adult phrasing.
The content of the child's statements is commented on, including allegations and key event details, without inferring truthfulness.
Audio-only behavioral observations are noted, such as the child's affect, tone, pauses, and emotional shifts related to specific topics.
A section on forensic consistency and reliability considers factors like internal consistency, developmental appropriateness, and evidence of coaching or compliance, explicitly avoiding a credibility determination.
Potential interview contamination issues are identified, including leading prompts, repeated questioning, introduction of new information by the interviewer, and pressure.
Key, high-value forensic statements are extracted verbatim from the transcript.
Finally, the analysis identifies gaps and limitations, such as unclear timelines, ambiguous references, incomplete narratives, or audio quality issues.

name: Domestic Violence Adult Protection Case Opening Assessment Form
author: Velum
description: Suitable for social workers to record domestic violence home visits. Converts violence history and needs into a structured assessment form to assist in formulating personal safety and emotional support plans.
body:
The case involves a 72-year-old female case subject who, after long-term psychological and economic violence from her 45-year-old youngest son—demanding money and shouting insults after drinking—reported the case, hoping to constrain the respondent’s behavior through a protection order.
The case subject lives with her eldest daughter. The respondent is the youngest son, unmarried and with unstable employment, with a drinking problem. After drinking, he often asks to borrow money and a vehicle; upon refusal, he shouts at the door. This behavior has lasted for more than 15 years.
The case subject believes the violence stems from the respondent’s suspected mental illness, alcohol abuse, and poor economic condition. Her current coping method is locking the door to avoid interaction, and she recognizes the need to call the police or seek help from the eldest daughter after the respondent drinks to ensure safety.
After the case subject reported to the police for the first time, the police agency assisted with notification and application for a protection order, and she agreed to social affairs agency involvement; the respondent’s behavior has eased after the report but expressed dissatisfaction.
The case subject’s current needs are personal safety (protection order application), emotional support, and legal issues (court accompaniment). Her strengths include informal support from her eldest daughter and seniors at the community center, as well as formal resources from police and social affairs; barriers include being alone at home during the day and a lack of other family assistance.
The service plan aims to obtain a protection order within three months to ensure personal safety, and provide emotional support and enhance self-affirmation through regular home visits, phone check-ins, and court accompaniment.

name: Employee Relations Investigation Summary
author: Velum
description: Turn a meeting transcript into a neutral HR case note with timeline, evidence, and next steps.
body:
The primary purpose is to create a confidential, neutral, and factual employee relations investigation summary for internal HR use at Colorado Coalition for the Homeless (CCH), based on meeting recordings or transcripts to support internal review and decision-making.
The summary must begin with standardized case information, including case name, relevant dates, participants, department, and the type of matter being investigated.
It requires a concise summary of the allegation or concern, detailing who raised it against whom, what allegedly occurred, and the dates, locations, and immediate impacts involved.
The scope of the investigation must be defined by listing specific issues as neutral questions, such as whether a certain conduct occurred or if a policy was followed.
A timeline of relevant events mentioned must be created, with each entry including the date, a description of the event, and the source of the information.
The statement from the complainant or reporting party must be summarized, covering key allegations, examples, named witnesses, prior reporting attempts, and desired outcomes.
The respondent's statement, if applicable, should be summarized, including their response to each allegation, any denials or clarifications, and context provided.
Statements from each witness must be summarized separately, detailing what they directly observed versus what they heard secondhand, and any evidence they referenced.
All referenced evidence, such as emails, records, or policies, must be listed with a description, date, and its current review status.
A clear distinction must be made between facts that are established and corroborated versus those that are disputed, unclear, or require further verification.
The summary should identify any company policies or processes that may be implicated by the events, using cautious wording without concluding that a violation occurred.
Any immediate interim actions taken or recommended for risk management, such as separating parties or preserving evidence, must be documented.
The analysis section must provide an evidence-based assessment of what supports or contradicts the allegations, what remains unresolved, and any credibility considerations discussed.
A preliminary finding status (substantiated, unsubstantiated, or inconclusive) should be assigned to each major allegation only if the available information supports it.
The document must outline practical next steps, including the action, owner, and purpose, such as interviewing more witnesses or consulting with HR leadership.
Any discussions regarding retaliation concerns or confidentiality instructions given during the meeting must be noted.
Finally, the summary should include documentation notes specifying its purpose (e.g., working notes) and whether further formal documentation is required.

name: SBA INTERVIEW
author: Velum
description: Extracts testimonials and product insights from interviews. Identifies user behavior and gaps.
body:
This document provides a comprehensive framework for analyzing beta test feedback interviews for an AI advisory product, THE BOARD, to generate multi-perspective insights on product-market fit.
Collect 5-7 direct quotes for testimonials, focusing on emotional impact, quantified value, identity transformation, comparisons, and referral language, noting the context that prompted each statement.
Identify and rank the top five value propositions by analyzing the specific problem solved, time saved, emotional benefits conferred, comparisons made, and any signals indicating a willingness to pay.
Analyze the user's psychological profile by examining identity shifts, hidden anxieties like imposter syndrome, emotional triggers for excitement or frustration, and social dynamics related to status and professional image, as well as attachment patterns formed with the AI.
Evaluate product-market fit by scoring problem-solution fit, the "must-have" nature of the product, advocacy potential, expansion possibilities, and stickiness, supporting each score with direct evidence from the interview.
Document user behavior and workflow by identifying setup friction, the first question asked, usage frequency, primary use cases, and how the product integrates with their existing processes.
Gather pricing and monetization insights by noting direct willingness-to-pay statements, indirect value indicators, price anchors mentioned, and signals of budget authority to determine the buyer profile.
Identify critical gaps and objections by capturing missing features, points of confusion, suggestions for improvement, mentioned competitive alternatives, and potential reasons for user churn.
Uncover channel and expansion opportunities by noting other potential users, unintended use cases, partnership possibilities, and industry-specific applications mentioned by the user.
Capture verbatim gems, such as revealing metaphors, repeated phrases, and emotional exclamations, that highlight deep user truths and unexpected applications.
Evaluate the interviewer's effectiveness by noting which questions yielded breakthroughs, identifying missed follow-up opportunities, and analyzing shifts in interview energy to improve future sessions.
Create a summary scorecard to provide an overall rating of the beta tester, including their testimonial value, product champion potential, revenue potential, feedback quality, and follow-up priority.
Define clear action items based on the analysis, including immediate follow-ups, suggested product improvements, necessary documentation, and questions for subsequent sessions.
Document any red flags or concerning signals observed during the interview regarding the product, market, or overall approach.

name: Recruitment Interview for Self-Employed Agents
author: Velum
description: Create an official ECC interview report. Records Q&A, strengths, concerns, actions, decision.
body:
This document provides a structured template for creating an official ECC Endorsement Interview Report for the National Association of Evangelicals (NAE) Chaplaincy Division, which will become part of the candidate's permanent file.
The report must begin by documenting fundamental interview details, including the date, location/method, interviewer, interviewee, and the type of interview being conducted.
It requires a summary of the applicant's background, covering their current ministry, employer, church affiliation, ordination status, relevant military or chaplaincy experience, and family information if discussed.
The report must clearly identify the specific chaplaincy position for which endorsement is requested, including the type of chaplaincy, employing organization, and setting.
A section on educational qualifications is required to document degrees, institutions, Clinical Pastoral Education (CPE), remaining requirements, and professional certifications to verify that educational standards are met.
All significant interview questions and the applicant's corresponding responses must be recorded verbatim and in the order they were asked.
Information shared by the interviewer, such as details about the ECC endorsement process, requirements, policies, and any advice or resources provided, must be summarized.
The applicant's strengths, such as their calling, maturity, experience, and skills, should be identified and supported with evidence from the interview.
Any concerns or areas needing follow-up related to the applicant's education, experience, theology, character, or administrative requirements must be detailed, or it should be stated that no significant concerns were found.
A list of specific action items is required, detailing all responsibilities and follow-up tasks agreed upon by both the applicant and the ECC/interviewer.
The "Endorser's Notes" section is for capturing only the interviewer's direct observations, comments, and rationale spoken during the interview, without adding any new opinions or conclusions.
An overall evaluation must provide a balanced assessment of the applicant's ministry and educational qualifications, readiness for chaplaincy, strengths, and any remaining requirements.
The report must conclude with a clear endorsement decision—"Endorse," "Endorse Pending Completion of Requirements," or "Do Not Endorse"—along with the supporting reasons and any specific conditions.
A concise, one-paragraph executive summary must be included to provide a quick overview of the applicant, position, qualifications, strengths, concerns, and final recommendation for future file review.

name: Intervener EAA Model
author: Velum
description: For dental HR. Records and scores by level. Generates report with profile and recommendation.
body:
This document defines a structured job interview for Dental Mechanics, guided by an HR assistant, which includes a scoring and automatic evaluation system to determine candidate suitability.
Initially, general applicant data is collected, such as name, age, city, years of experience, and whether they work in their own or an external laboratory.
The fixed prosthesis wax-ups section evaluates the candidate's experience, whether they use traditional or digital techniques, the types of work they perform, and their self-declared level to assign a score.
Experience with complete dentures, removable partials, metal frameworks, and conventional acrylic is inquired about, concluding with a score assigned based on the candidate's level.
The evaluation of experience with Deflex-type injection includes questions about years of practice, brands used, whether they perform the complete or partial process, and a score assignment based on the declared level.
In the fixed prosthesis area, it is asked if they perform porcelain build-up, the materials they use (metal, zirconia, disilicate), if they do staining, glazing, and full layering, assigning a score for their level.
The ability to make bruxism splints is evaluated, asking about the technique and materials used, and the candidate's proficiency level is scored.
It is verified if the applicant makes stamped plates, if the process is complete or partial, and a score is assigned according to their level of mastery.
The surgical guides section determines if the candidate produces them, whether they are digital, printed, or conventional, if they plan or just print, and a score is assigned.
Competence in digital planning software such as ExoCAD, Blue Sky Plan, Blender, and Meshmixer is evaluated, along with years of digital experience, their main uses, and an overall score is assigned.
An appendix section is included for the candidate to detail any other skills, techniques, equipment, or additional software they master.
At the close, questions are asked about availability, salary expectations, and a final comment from the applicant is requested.
The automatic evaluation system calculates a total score out of 24 points (8 areas), classifying the candidate as Junior (0-10), Intermediate (11-17), or Advanced (18-24).
Finally, an automatic report is generated including a technical summary, strengths, areas to reinforce, the candidate's overall level, and a final hiring recommendation.

name: Junior Project Manager - 2nd Round Technical Interview Scorecard
author: Velum
description: 30–45 min scorecard for 2nd-round junior PM interviews. Rate 7 skills 1–5 and note concerns.
body:
The document outlines the structure, content, and scoring for a 30-45 minute second-round technical interview for a Junior Project Manager, focusing on technical judgment, planning, communication, and coachability with a total possible score of 35.
The project planning and scheduling section assesses the candidate's ability to create a project schedule from contract to construction, determine task dependencies and the critical path, and respond to material lead time issues that conflict with the construction start date.
The budgeting and cost control section questions the candidate on their methods for tracking project costs against the budget, their process for validating and approving subcontractor change orders, and their ability to recognize early warning signs of potential budget overruns.
The risk and issue management portion evaluates the candidate's understanding of the difference between a project risk and an issue, and their ability to describe a past experience where they identified, documented, and communicated a problem early.
The communication and documentation section probes the candidate's judgment on what information requires formal documentation versus verbal communication, and their role as a mediator when on-site disagreements arise between stakeholders like a superintendent and a designer.
The tools, systems, and organization part of the interview tests the candidate's practical experience with project management software for schedules and budgets, and their personal strategies for organizing their work week while managing multiple projects.
The change management section assesses how the candidate handles client change requests that impact cost and schedule, and the processes they use to prevent unapproved changes from being incorporated into the project.
The judgment and growth section evaluates the candidate's self-awareness regarding their weakest technical area and their plan for improvement, as well as their judgment on when to escalate an issue versus solving it independently.
A scored evaluation rubric is used to rate the candidate on a 1-5 scale across seven competencies: Project Planning, Budget Awareness, Risk Management, Change Management, Communication, Tools/Systems, and Judgment/Coachability.
A scoring summary provides hiring recommendations based on the candidate's total score: 32-35 for a Strong Hire, 28-31 for a Hire, 24-27 for a panel discussion, and below 24 to not proceed.

name: RPBDC session
author: Velum
description: Log candidate answers to score logic, teamwork, and stress for clear hiring recommendations.
body:
This Aptitude & Reasoning Evaluation Template facilitates systematic candidate evaluation.
Candidate Information section requires details such as Candidate Name, Position Applied For, Interview Date, Interviewer Name, and Duration of Aptitude Round.
Aptitude Question 1 involves recording the question, candidate's response, correctness of the answer, and evaluating problem-solving skills, logical thinking, decision making, time taken, understanding of the problem, and approach to the solution.
Aptitude Question 2 follows the same structure as Aptitude Question 1 for assessing candidate performance.
Aptitude Question 3 also requires recording the question, candidate's response, correctness of the answer, and evaluating problem-solving skills, logical thinking, decision making, time taken, understanding of the problem, and approach to the solution.
Behavioral & Logical Thinking Assessment observes if the candidate approached questions logically, asked for clarification or assumed, their confidence, how well they broke down complex problems, and their problem-solving approach.
Decision-Making & Problem-Solving Process section involves entering a question related to decision-making or a real-time scenario, the candidate's response, correctness of the answer, and evaluating logical decision-making, time taken, approach to solution, and ability to handle complex problems.
Collaborative Skills section requires a situational question about teamwork, the candidate's response, willingness to collaborate, communication skills with the team, interaction with the interviewer, and ability to work with other developers.
Time Management & Stress Handling observation assesses how well the candidate managed time, handled time pressure, exhibited stress, and their stress management rating.
Communication Skills observation focuses on clarity of expressed thoughts, explanation of problem-solving approaches, confidence in communication, and ability to present ideas effectively.
Overall Evaluation requires assessing suitability for the role, identifying strengths and weaknesses, and rating problem-solving capability, decision-making ability, team collaboration skills, communication skills, time management and stress handling, and overall performance.
Final Decision section includes a yes/no for moving forward with the candidate and a detailed reason for the decision based on performance.
Conclusion provides final thoughts summarizing the candidate's performance and whether they demonstrated necessary skills, along with a recommendation for next steps.
The Rating Legend defines the scale from 1-10 for evaluations, categorizing performance levels from "Needs significant improvement" to "Excellent".

name: Interview Report
author: Velum
description: From a transcription, fills out the MMA Car Pros collection. Puts “Not specified” if absent.
body:
The objective is to produce a structured information collection for an MMA "Car Pros" insurance contract, based on the transcription of an interview with a professional and strictly adhering to official MMA documents and the Insurance Code.
Company identification: Collect basic company information, including company name, legal representative, legal form, registration dates and codes (SIREN/SIRET), NAF code, and CNPA membership.
Declared professional activity: Precisely define the main activity (based on the highest turnover), secondary activities (>30% of turnover), and ancillary activities (<30% of turnover) according to the MMA nomenclature, checking for the absence of excluded activities.
Operating locations: Specify the number and address of operating locations, occupancy status (tenant, owner), area, and total workforce, noting that Regional Directorate validation is required if the workforce exceeds 10 people.
Economic data: Collect the last annual turnover excl. tax, its breakdown by activity if possible, and check if the last three financial years have been profitable.
Claims history for the last 36 months: Detail the claims history for RC/Property Damage/Business Interruption (General Liability, Property Damage, Business Interruption) guarantees and for vehicles, specifying the period and whether a prior termination occurred.
Previous insurance situation: Identify the previous insurer, contract number, guarantees in place, and whether managers' personal vehicles should be included in the new contract.
Civil Liability (RC): Determine the needs for General Liability and Professional Liability, the value of entrusted goods, the existence of classified installations (ICPE), recent legal proceedings, and the desire for D&O liability for corporate officers.
Property damage: Declare the total area to be insured, the capital for real estate and operating movable property, as well as for archives. Specify the presence of risky activities such as bodywork, storage of plastic foams or tires.
Business Interruption (BI): Define whether the BI guarantee is desired, its formula (fixed or actual), the amount of compensation and its duration, as well as the possible coverage of the loss of goodwill value.
Mentioned complementary guarantees: List other guarantees discussed during the interview, such as theft, machinery breakdown, legal protection or new for old value.
Contractual vigilance points: Note elements requiring particular attention, such as sensitive activities, incomplete declarations or cases requiring Regional Directorate validation.
Actions to follow and summary: Define the next steps for the MMA agency (information to be completed, documents to be requested, file study) and write a factual operational summary for quick decision-making by the underwriting department.

name: Hiring Profile
author: Velum
description: Analyzes interviews with DISC profile and cultural fit. Summarizes risks and potentials to support selection.
body:
The objective is to generate a complete report for the decision-making regarding the hiring of an associate lawyer, using a prompt that instructs an AI to act as a multidisciplinary technical jury to analyze an interview.
The analysis should begin with the candidate's general profile, evaluating their predominant archetype, emotional maturity, self-awareness, professional posture, and ambition.
It is necessary to evaluate the candidate's decision-making style, determining whether it is rational or emotional, based on data or impressions, and the clarity and coherence of their reasoning.
The report must include an analysis of the candidate's DISC profile (Dominance, Influence, Steadiness, Conscientiousness), with justifications, identifying the predominant quadrant and the potential risks and benefits in the legal environment.
The candidate's predominant representational system (Visual, Auditory, or Kinesthetic - VAC) must be identified, along with the words and patterns that support the conclusion and how they process information.
Communication and verbal behavior should be evaluated in terms of assertiveness, clarity, capacity for synthesis, confidence, and ability to structure complex arguments.
The candidate's emotional intelligence will be analyzed based on their self-control, empathy, resilience, ability to handle pressure, and emotional stability.
The technical and behavioral legal profile will be evaluated, considering the strength of argumentation, critical thinking, perceived technical potential, autonomy, adherence to litigation or consulting, and professional maturity.
Cultural fit with a high-performance firm will be verified, identifying adherence to the culture, collaborative posture, openness to feedback, growth mindset, and ethical conduct.
The report should list the behavioral, emotional, technical, and cultural incompatibility risks associated with the candidate.
The candidate's strengths and potentials should be highlighted, including competitive differentiators, notable skills, development opportunities, and how they would add value to the team.
A final opinion should be issued, containing a recommendation (hire, hire with reservations, do not hire) with technical justification and guidance on how to lead, integrate, and allocate the candidate if hired.

name: Assessment Sheet
author: Velum
description: From a transcript, extract and structure. Generate summary, skills, expectations, opinion.
body:
The mission is to act as a senior recruiter to produce a professional and structured candidate brief for a client, based solely on an interview transcript.
The report must begin with candidate identification, including information such as name, position, location, availability, and languages, stating "Not specified" if information is missing.
An executive summary of 15 to 20 lines should provide a quick overview of the profile, covering seniority, sectors, expertise, leadership style, results, added value, motivations, and points of vigilance.
Technical skills (hard skills) must be listed with clarification of their source (observed, self-declared, unconfirmed) and illustrated with an example.
Behavioral skills (soft skills) must be listed, distinguishing between observed and self-declared ones, each supported by a concrete example from the interview.
The report should present between 5 and 8 major strengths of the candidate, formulated as selling points for the client, with a clear title, a short explanation, and a concrete example.
It must also list 4 to 6 areas for development or points of vigilance in a factual tone, describing the potential risk for the company and the conditions under which it could become a problem.
The candidate's professional motivations must be identified and classified by priority, specifying evidence from the interview and the risk if this driver is not activated.
Candidate expectations regarding the position, management, company, environment, and career trajectory must be presented in a structured manner.
Potential concerns, expressed fears, weak signals, or inconsistencies that could hinder job acceptance must be identified.
A hypothetical psychological analysis based on the interview is required, using the Big Five (Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness, Emotional Stability) and DISC (Dominance, Influence, Steadiness, Conscientiousness) models presented separately.
The report must describe the ideal conditions for the candidate's success, including the type of management, autonomy, pace, company culture, and team.
Salary expectations and associated conditions (current and desired salary, variable, benefits, flexibility) must be clearly stated, or marked as "Not specified".
The recruiter's opinion must conclude the report by evaluating the level of fit for the position (Low, Moderate, Good, Excellent) and highlighting a maximum of three major points of vigilance.
A list of remaining questions and information to clarify in a future interview must be established to complete the candidate evaluation.

name: Annual Performance Review Preparation Grid Generation
author: Velum
description: Turn a family interview into record of people, dates, places, stories, quotes. Keeps details clear.
body:
The primary goal is to create a detailed archival record of a family-history conversation, preserving all distinct facts for future family research, rather than a brief summary.
A "Recording Overview" section should capture the interview subject and interviewer's names, recording date, main topics discussed, and a brief description of the conversation.
The "People Mentioned" section requires creating a separate subsection for every individual, detailing their name, relationships, life details, personal characteristics, and significant events or stories associated with them.
The "Chronological Family History" section must arrange all datable events in sequence, using exact dates when known and approximate periods otherwise, without inventing information.
A "Places and Properties" section should list every mentioned location, including details about who was there, its appearance, events that occurred, and any changes over time.
The "Distinct Memories and Stories" section is for capturing each story as a separate entry, detailing the people involved, time, location, events, and emotional significance.
The "Family Relationships and Connections" section should list all described or implied relationships, including familial, social, and professional ties, while noting any uncertainties.
"Customs, Daily Life and Family Culture" is a section for documenting details about meals, holidays, religious practices, work, social norms, and everyday life.
The "Historical Context" section is for identifying larger historical events or social conditions as mentioned in the recording, using only the information provided.
A "Questions and Unresolved Details" section should list potential transcription errors, conflicting accounts, uncertain information, and follow-up questions for future interviews.
The "Quotable Passages" section should include memorable statements that capture the speaker's personality or perspective, quoted faithfully from the transcript.
A final "Complete Fact Inventory" section must provide a numbered list of every single distinct factual detail from the recording, prioritizing completeness over brevity.
Throughout the document, it is critical to preserve uncertainty, avoid inventing information, distinguish between fact and speculation, retain contradictory versions, and use the speaker's original terminology.

name: Business Psyche Assessment
author: Velum
description: Paste a conversation for a leadership profile with examples and growth tips. Flags risks.
body:
The primary objective is to conduct a comprehensive psychological and leadership assessment by analyzing a conversation across thirteen specific dimensions.
Assess tribal leadership stage (2-5) through observable language patterns (e.g., 'I' vs. 'we'), relationship structures (dyadic vs. triadic), and focus on team versus self, gauging value alignment with collective outcomes.
Identify core motivations by distinguishing between intrinsic drivers like autonomy and purpose, and extrinsic needs such as recognition and financial reward, to understand what energizes or depletes the individual.
Analyze fears and avoidance patterns by identifying core anxieties (e.g., failure, rejection) and observing how they manifest as defensive behaviors under stress, revealing psychological safety needs.
Evaluate identity and self-perception by comparing how individuals describe their role and stated values against their demonstrated actions and growth indicators, noting any gap between their current and aspirational self.
Determine the individual's sense of control and agency by assessing their locus of control (internal vs. external), comfort with decision-making autonomy, and belief in their ability to influence outcomes.
Examine relational dynamics by observing their attachment style, conflict response patterns (e.g., avoid, collaborate), orientation towards collaboration versus competition, and trust-building behaviors.
Understand stress and security responses by noting behavioral shifts under pressure, identifying resilience indicators, coping mechanisms, and specific triggers versus grounding factors.
Assess communication and problem-solving skills through their emotional regulation, level of problem ownership, focus on future solutions versus past issues, and demonstrated action orientation.
Evaluate psychological safety contribution across four levels: Inclusion, Learner, Contributor, and Challenger Safety, by observing how their presence affects the team's willingness to be vulnerable, ask questions, share ideas, and disagree productively.
Identify patterns of team dysfunction by looking for behavioral examples related to trust, conflict, commitment, accountability, and a focus on collective results versus individual status.
Analyze dynamics with authority and decision-making by observing deference patterns, preferred involvement level in decisions, ability to influence upwards, and whether they seek empowerment or permission.
Assess the individual's discretion level by analyzing where they seek permission versus act independently, the alignment of their capability with their authority, and their comfort with ambiguity.
Evaluate alignment with team practices by observing their contribution to team culture, information-sharing habits, and whether they support peers or position themselves competitively.
The analysis requires providing specific conversational examples for each dimension, flagging contradictions between stated and demonstrated patterns, identifying development opportunities, and assessing overall leadership readiness and team impact.

name: GPT1
author: Velum
description: Helps therapists organize transcriptions into structured and faithful clinical documents.
body:
The main objective is to transform a psychotherapeutic interview transcript into a structured and usable clinical document for the therapist, by reformulating and synthesizing the content without interpretation or addition.
General instructions require strictly adhering to the content of the transcript, adopting a professional and concise style, eliminating superfluous elements of oral language, and producing a text that appears to be written by the psychologist himself.
The document structure must systematically include nine sections: Session Context, What the patient spontaneously brings, Emotional and relational posture, Subjective stakes, Evolution since the previous session, Work done, Therapeutic axes, Proposed avenues, and Follow-up indicators.
The "Session Context" section must specify the number, date, session setting, presence of third parties, and the expressed objective or general atmosphere.
The "What the patient spontaneously brings" section must highlight the main theme, dominant emotions, expectations, and concrete situations reported.
The "Emotional and relational posture of the moment" section must describe the affective tone, signs of tension or openness, evoked bodily sensations, and narrative movements based solely on the patient's words.
The "Subjective stakes and underlying dynamics" section must concisely synthesize the internal conflicts, implicit needs, and recurring themes of suffering derived from the discourse.
The "Evolution since the previous session" section should only be filled if the patient mentions changes, insights, new behaviors, or resistances.
The "Work done during the session" section must describe the key questions, reformulations, exercises, elements worked on, and significant moments of the session.
The "Current therapeutic axes" section must synthesize the orientations worked on, the immediate objectives formulated from the patient's words, and positive support points.
The "Proposed avenues or therapeutic tasks" section must list only the observation avenues, experiments, or follow-up questions actually evoked during the interview.
The "Follow-up indicators" section must note the signs to observe for the next session, expected developments, and points of vigilance expressed by the patient.
Important rules stipulate never to interpret, to reformulate sensitive content without altering it, to maintain a sober tone, and to produce a synthesis of 15 to 25 lines, omitting sections for which no information is available.
The output format requires visible section titles, short and readable paragraphs, and the complete absence of meta-comments or reminders of instructions.

name: Architectural Interview Writing
author: Velum
description: Suitable for organizing architect interviews, transforming scattered records into aesthetic and professional reports for various publishing and digital platforms.
body:
The task is to transform the recorded content of an architect's interview into fluent, professional, and aesthetically pleasing Chinese feature articles, suitable for print or digital publication.
Must understand the architect's interview content, including architectural concepts, site design, construction supervision, material selection, user space interaction, client communication, and regional considerations.
Must translate design logic and implicit emotions into text that is easy for general readers to understand and engaging.
Writing should maintain a professional tone while preserving the speaker's personal style and rhythm.
Ensure all sentences are grammatically correct and fluent, using vocabulary customary in Taiwan.
Paragraph structure should be clear and easy to read, suitable for editing and publishing.
Word choice should be refined but not pretentious, avoiding excessive embellishment or abstraction.
May correct obvious grammatical, logical, or repetitive errors in the interview.
If dialogue is fragmented or unclear, meaning may be reconstructed according to context, but information must not be fabricated.
Article structure is recommended to include a concise introduction (such as setting the scene, a quote, or background explanation).
The main structure can adopt a Q&A format; questions may be simplified or restated for clarity.
If the transcript is too chaotic, it can be rewritten in a narrative interview format, clearly indicating the speaker's tone.
Paragraphs should remain short, recommended at 4 to 6 lines each for readability.
Style should be 80% practical and professional, incorporating architectural vocabulary, and 20% emotional expression or imagination.
Writing should be clear and informative, while maintaining sensitivity and fluency.
Avoid overly poetic or dramatic expressions, ensuring a natural connection between speaker and reader.
Finally, automatically conduct a complete check of grammar, punctuation, and formatting to ensure no typos, repetition, or inconsistencies.

name: Older Child FTF Case Management Narrative (Child Welfare)
author: Velum
description: Paste a monthly FTF visit recording. Get a third-person case narrative with set headers.
body:
Primary purpose is to provide structured guidelines for generating comprehensive, objective child welfare case management documentation for monthly face-to-face visits based on audio recordings.
General writing requirements mandate a third-person professional caseworker narrative mimicking a specific style, utilizing detailed paragraphs, consistent naming conventions, objective language, explicit notation of unaddressed topics, and specific transitional phrases.
The required contact metadata header must accurately capture logistical details including personnel, date, time, duration, purpose, contact method, announcement status, sibling visit inclusion, location, and principals or collaterals involved.
Initial visit observations require a detailed description of the arrival, attendees, environmental conditions, meeting privacy, and the child's physical appearance, clothing, demeanor, and interactions.
Family contact and visitation documentation must address parent and sibling interactions, contact frequency and methods, desired connections, upcoming visits, and the child's emotional responses before, during, and after visits.
Educational needs documentation covers school information, grade level, attendance, academic performance, teacher input, special school services, and the child's feelings regarding education.
Adjustment and well-being reporting includes the child's adaptation to placement, understanding of being in care, emotional presentation, coping skills, behavioral concerns, cultural needs, and overall functioning.
Medical and dental needs sections detail current health status, illnesses, medications, appointments, sleep habits, appetite, physical hygiene, and any pending health services.
Therapeutic needs and services reporting addresses counseling participation, therapy frequency, psychological or psychiatric evaluations, treatment progress, recommendations, and caregiver support.
Placement and safety documentation requires an extensive narrative on caregiver and household relationships, safety assessments, home and bedroom observations, discipline methods, behavioral issues, and the child's stated sense of safety.
Permanency goal and case status sections outline the child's understanding of the case, primary and concurrent goals, court updates, service plan progress, relative developments, and reunification efforts.
Transitional planning applies exclusively to children aged 16 or older, detailing life skills, housing, education, and employment goals, while requiring a specific standardized exclusion statement for younger children.
Social and emotional needs documentation focuses on peer relationships, recreational and extracurricular activities, community or church involvement, hobbies, socialization opportunities, and positive emotional supports.

name: Job Profile Alignment
author: Velum
description: Suitable for recruiters to align requirements. Through guided dialogue, it helps organize job positioning, competency matrices, and assessment standards to quickly form accurate recruitment documents.
body:
This document provides a structured dialogue framework, aiming to help companies clarify strategic role needs, build accurate candidate profiles, define success standards, and predict risks through systematic questioning.
The core objectives of the dialogue are to clarify the strategic positioning and true needs of the role, build a verifiable candidate profile, identify potential risks and room for compromise, and establish clear success paths and evaluation criteria.
Role positioning requires clarifying its basic information (name, reporting line, team, level), and delving into whether the recruitment background is for replacement, new establishment, or upgrade, while also considering alternative plans if the position cannot be filled in the short term.
Building a candidate profile involves deconstructing hard thresholds (years of experience, industry background, educational background), core competency matrix (essential skills and knowledge), soft skills and traits (personality, driving force, stress resistance, cultural fit), and compensation incentive plans.
The success path and evaluation criteria for the role need to clarify the business background and challenges, set 30/60/90-day onboarding milestones, define annual core objectives (KPI/OKR), and explain available resources and support systems.
The risk prediction section aims to identify hidden problems in recruitment, clarify the room for compromise between ideal and realistic profiles, assess the potential for candidate development, and clarify promotion paths and other additional information.
The recommended dialogue process is divided into three rounds: the first round quickly reviews all sections, the second round delves into ambiguous or contradictory points, and the third round organizes the content into a standard document to reach consensus.

name: WCPD Interview
author: Velum
description: For interviews. Input a recording: timeline, speakers, summary, transcript, action plan.
body:
Spartan Investigations requires structured investigative documentation for recordings, covering case context, event chronology, participants, conversation substance, transcript overview, actions, observations, recommended follow-up, and final case relevance.
Case overview captures the recording purpose, date, time, subject matter, available case name or reference number, and conversation type such as interview, surveillance debrief, client meeting, witness statement, or operational coordination.
Timeline of events organizes significant moments in chronological order, including timestamps, transitions, turning points, and points where actions, instructions, or events are mentioned or agreed upon.
Speaker identification and roles label each participant by name or role, define relevance to the investigation, and clearly mark speaker changes in summaries and transcripts.
Conversation summary organizes discussion by topic and subtopic, preserving logical order while capturing main statements, questions, clarifications, conflicting information, evidence-related dialogue, and references to people, locations, vehicles, or incidents.
Transcript overview provides cleaned, readable exchange summaries with approximate timestamps that give context for each statement or interaction.
After-action summary documents the discussion outcome, decided actions, responsible parties, assignments, follow-up items, operational directives, next investigative steps, deadlines, and pending verification points.
Observations and analysis record relevant investigator observations, behavioral notes, tone, inconsistencies, potential leads, investigative red flags, and intelligence indicators when applicable.
Recommended action plan lists follow-up steps for evidence gathering, interviews, or surveillance, with responsible parties, estimated completion times, and supporting details.
Closing summary states the overall findings, tone, outcome, and whether the conversation supports, contradicts, or expands existing case information.
Formatting requirements call for clear section headers, bullet formatting, investigative professionalism, factual neutrality, evidence-based observations, and the final label “CONFIDENTIAL – INVESTIGATOR USE ONLY.”
Example closing line states that the report is generated for official investigative documentation and entered into the case file as part of the ongoing inquiry under Spartan Investigations & Executive Protection.

name: INTERVIEW TEMPLATE WITH TIMESTAMPS
author: Velum
description: Summarizes interview recording into Q&A, strengths, and gaps. Notes what they valued and next prep.
body:
The primary goal is to analyze an interview recording from the interviewee's perspective to objectively assess their performance and prepare for subsequent rounds.
The analysis should include an overview of the interview, detailing the company, role, stage, interviewers, purpose, and main themes.
It requires a detailed breakdown of questions asked, summarizing the candidate's answers and evaluating their effectiveness with a brief explanation.
The candidate's three to five strongest answers must be identified, explaining what was said, why it was effective, the capability demonstrated, and any compelling metrics used.
Answers that were weak or could be improved—such as those that were too long, vague, or not responsive—need to be identified, with suggestions for improvement.
A list of all career examples, stories, and metrics used during the interview should be compiled, noting the specific competency each one demonstrated.
The analysis must interpret the interviewer's priorities, concerns, and valued skills based on their questions and comments.
An assessment of the candidate's communication style is required, covering aspects like confidence, executive presence, conciseness, and ability to convey business value.
The summary should identify any positive hiring signals or potential red flags from the interviewer that could influence the hiring decision.
It needs to list the questions the candidate asked, summarize what was learned, and note any important questions that were missed.
The output must provide specific follow-up opportunities for a thank-you note or future interviews, including points to clarify or reinforce.
A quantitative scorecard (1-10) is required for overall performance, executive presence, communication, experience, business acumen, role fit, and persuasiveness, each with a brief explanation.
The analysis should conclude with the top five most important takeaways from the interview.
To prepare for the next round, the analysis must provide the five most likely future questions, three essential career stories to prepare, three areas for improved positioning, and five intelligent questions to ask.
For enterprise sales roles, the evaluation must specifically assess the candidate's ability to sell to C-level executives, manage complex accounts, and demonstrate quantifiable results.

name: HCPN Finishing Cohort Assessments
author: Velum
description: Paste a planter/spouse transcript. Get fit review, flags, needs, and a recommendation.
body:
The primary purpose of the HCPN Finishing Cohort Assessment is to analyze a transcript from a prospective church planter and spouse to determine their fitness for the program in the current season, focusing on readiness, cultural fit, health, and various leadership and missional capacities.
An overall summary should be provided, covering concise yet insightful impressions of the planter, the spouse, their dynamic, and the overall assessment outcome.
The couple's fit for the HCPN Finishing Cohort is assessed based on their humility, relational warmth, theological alignment, collaborative posture, emotional maturity, coachability, developmental posture, and suitability for Houston's church planting culture, distinguishing between strengths, concerns, and unresolved questions.
The assessment evaluates the couple's missional impulse by examining their evangelistic instinct, engagement with non-Christians, missionary lifestyle, and burden for the lost, looking for specific evidence of relationships and gospel conversations rather than vague aspirations.
Spiritual formation is assessed by examining current habits like prayer, Scripture engagement, spiritual rhythms, self-awareness, and accountability, to determine if ministry flows from spiritual overflow or from depletion and performance.
The health of the marriage and family is evaluated by assessing spousal unity, emotional honesty, stress patterns, conflict resolution, and sustainability for planting life, paying close attention to the spouse's engagement and any signs of disconnect or exhaustion.
The couple's leadership and ministry philosophy are assessed for maturity, disciple-making ability, theological clarity, resilience to criticism, and a multiplication mindset, looking for evidence of developing leaders and collaborative practices.
Coachability and a developmental posture are evaluated by assessing teachability, humility, self-awareness, and openness to challenge, while watching for signs of defensiveness, excessive certainty, or an inability to acknowledge weakness.
The analysis requires identifying the top 3–5 practical and specific areas where the planter or couple needs the most growth, coaching, or support.
The process includes listing "Green Flags," which are the strongest positive indicators of readiness, maturity, HCPN fit, and healthy leadership potential.
"Yellow/Red Flags" must be identified, listing concerns such as vague spirituality, spousal hesitation, defensiveness, or a lack of evangelistic engagement, and distinguishing them as mild, significant, or potentially disqualifying.
A final, single recommendation must be made from a set list (Strong Recommend, Recommend, etc.), supported by a clear and pastoral explanation.
If the couple is accepted, the analysis should conclude by suggesting the top three coaching priorities for HCPN to focus on during their residency.
The tone for the analysis must be discerning, pastoral, concise, honest, and nuanced, avoiding flattery or assumptions without evidence, and clearly distinguishing between observed facts and interpretations.

name: Mattelsa. Retention interview. QUANTITATIVE
author: Velum
description: Organizes interview content on management responsibility and risk management by item, while maintaining specific episodes.
body:
Specifically summarize the organizational management interview results according to the items of Category 3 (Social Responsibility in Management), 4 (Risk Management), 5 (Staff and Organizational Capacity Building), and 7 (Organizational Activities for Key Issues of the Office).
Category 3 "Social Responsibility in Management" evaluates organizational initiatives regarding compliance with laws, norms, and ethics, protection of user rights, and contribution to local welfare. Specifically, it includes disseminating information to staff and confirming compliance, establishing systems for complaint resolution and abuse prevention, disclosing business activities, and participating in local networks.
Category 4 "Risk Management" evaluates the identification and prioritization of risks that hinder business continuity (accidents, infectious diseases, disasters, etc.), implementation of countermeasures, formulation and dissemination of a Business Continuity Plan (BCP), and analysis and recurrence prevention measures in case of occurrence. It also includes the establishment of information management regulations, setting access rights, and building a system compliant with the Personal Information Protection Law.
Category 5 "Staff and Organizational Capacity Building" evaluates initiatives for securing, developing, and retaining human resources required by the office. This includes formulating human resource development plans linked to clear career paths, conducting training, evaluating and reflecting development results, linking with treatment, creating a comfortable working environment, and building good interpersonal relationships among staff.
"Improvement of Organizational Strength" in Category 5 evaluates mechanisms for sharing individual staff learning across the organization, utilizing daily insights for business improvement, and initiatives to promote team goal achievement.
Category 7 "Organizational Activities for Key Issues of the Office" evaluates whether efforts and results for specific goals set in the previous year for key issues to realize the office's philosophy and basic policy are verified and reflected in improvement activities from this year onwards.

name: Comprehensive AOD Assessment Template
author: Velum
description: Organize client history, substance use, and mental health data into structured reports to assist in recovery planning.
body:
The template provides a structured approach for comprehensive drug and alcohol assessments, emphasizing objectivity and evidence-based reporting.
Introduction requires describing the client as a person, their reasons for assessment, and presenting issues, using respectful and objective language.
Personal History involves building a timeline of significant life events from childhood to the present, noting their impact on the client's development and current behaviors.
Whānau/Family History focuses on summarizing family dynamics, cultural identity, intergenerational patterns, and support systems, identifying protective and risk factors.
Substance Use History details the onset, progression, substances used, patterns, and associated harms, including the client's insights and previous change attempts.
Criminogenic section analyzes offending history, including types, frequency, and context, discussing dynamic and static risk factors within social, environmental, and psychological contexts.
Mental Health History documents diagnoses, symptoms, hospitalizations, treatments, and the impact of mental health on various life aspects, including medications.
Motivation to Change highlights internal and external motivators, client strengths, coping skills, and explores potential for engagement with recovery pathways.
Strengths and Problems List synthesizes a balanced view of client strengths and problems, framing strengths as assets for recovery and problems as intervention areas.
Clinical Diagnosis provides a clear, defensible summary of diagnoses with supporting evidence, using appropriate terminology and flagging any uncertainties.
Formulation integrates assessment information into a narrative using the 4Ps (Predisposing, Precipitating, Perpetuating, Protective factors) to explain behaviors.
Management Plan sets a roadmap for recovery with actionable items, including goals, needs for further assessment, medical treatments, pharmacotherapy, psychological therapy, whānau interventions, education options, and self-help groups.
Prognosis offers a realistic assessment of likely outcomes, discussing factors that could improve or worsen prognosis, framed hopefully but not over-optimistically.

name: BM Interview Template
author: Velum
description: Assess leadership and budget skills with ten questions. Evaluate candidate plans for the first 90 days.
body:
This interview template outlines 10 questions for a Branch Manager role, specifying the key talking points expected in a candidate's responses to evaluate their suitability.
The first question assesses a candidate's motivation by exploring how the role aligns with their career goals, their potential for impact, and their specific reasons for applying.
The second question evaluates leadership style by requesting a specific example of impactful leadership, their method for balancing approachability with accountability, and their view on critical leadership qualities for the role.
The third question examines performance management by asking about tools for tracking progress, motivational approaches for different personalities, and methods for celebrating wins and addressing setbacks.
The fourth question probes how a candidate handles underperformance by asking for a specific instance, focusing on the steps taken to find the root cause, communicate expectations, provide support, and the final outcome and lessons learned.
The fifth question tests decision-making under uncertainty by asking about key factors considered, how they respond when decisions go wrong, and whether they involve their team in the process.
The sixth question assesses budget management skills, specifically concerning cost control without sacrificing quality, the metrics used for tracking, and how they would forecast and adjust for business fluctuations.
