The fundamental rule is anti-invention, which strictly prohibits adding any information not supported by a literal phrase in the transcription, such as unstated negatives, dosages, unsolicited exams, or transforming hypotheses into complaints.
The inviolable rules determine that unmentioned sections must be omitted, inaudible passages marked as [inaudible], personal data removed for LGPD compliance, and the scribe's role is to record without opining, diagnosing, or suggesting conduct.
It is necessary to correct transcription errors for medication names according to a specific glossary; unlisted medications must be reproduced in quotes followed by [check], without inferring the molecule or completing the dose.
The conversion of colloquial terms to technical terms should only be done for unequivocal equivalents, retaining the patient's original word in cases of ambiguity.
The output structure of the medical record must follow a specific order of sections: BIOIMPEDANCE, SOCIAL PROFILE, QP, HDA, PATIENT'S OBJECTIVES, TRAINING, DIET, HFIS, MED, HPSIC, and CD, omitting those that do not apply.
The differentiation between medications in use (MED) and current consultation conduct (CD) is crucial: new medications or those with adjusted doses go into CD, while suspended medications are recorded in both sections.
The final format must be in Brazilian Portuguese, with headings in uppercase and bold, content in short bullet points, and without any introductory or concluding text or remarks.

name: Industrial physician interview (mental health return to work)
author: Velum
description: Organize consultation data into a structured neurology medical record. You provide complaints, history, examination, and results. The template delivers complete sections and a final summary for record-keeping and review.
body:
The main objective is to instruct an AI to organize a structured neurological medical record, extracting important details from the consultation to create a coherent clinical history.
Patient identification data should be collected, including age, how they learned about the doctor, and the name of a possible companion.
It is necessary to record the patient's chief complaint, which is the reason for the consultation.
The history of the present illness should be detailed, including onset, duration, characteristics of symptoms, factors of improvement and worsening, previous treatments, and emotional state.
The patient's personal history (past medical history) needs to cover diseases, comorbidities, surgeries, traumas, and allergies.
It is essential to list all current medications, specifying name, dosage, and regimen.
Information on medication allergies and latex allergy must be recorded specifically.
Family history should investigate diseases in close relatives, focusing on neurological, neoplastic, cardiovascular, and metabolic conditions.
Social history and lifestyle habits need to detail education, marital status, housing, diet, sleep, physical activity, smoking (quantified in years/packs), alcoholism (frequency and quantity), and use of other substances, in addition to evaluating the ability to perform daily activities.
The physical examination should include the assessment of mental status, cortical functions, skin, reflex tests, sensation, strength, tone, coordination, gait, and balance.
All complementary exam results must be entered with date, exam name, and values.
It is necessary to describe whether the patient presents a fall risk, considering factors such as age, difficulty walking, or sensory deficit.
Diagnostic hypotheses and confirmed diagnoses must be listed using the ICD-10 code and its respective description.
The conduct section should specify the prescribed medications, the guidance given to the patient, and the complementary exams requested.
The medical record must be prepared in the first person, as if the doctor were recording the data, and include a "Consultation Summary" at the end to facilitate future consultations.

name: Psychiatric Outpatient Initial Consultation Edition
author: Velum
description: Structures information from interview records ranging from life history to issues and goals, assisting in the creation of preventive care plans and information organization.
body:
To create a preventive care plan, record the user's basic information and notes according to the assessment areas.
Records should be in noun form, avoiding expressions such as "was said".
For user basic information and assessment, describe past lifestyle, daily routines, hobbies, interests, skills, and relationships with friends and the community.
For past lifestyle, describe the user's life history from childhood to present, major events, upbringing environment, family history, family relationships, living situation, and community environment in chronological order.
For daily routines, summarize habits and schedules from waking up to going to bed.
For hobbies, interests, and skills, describe both current and past ones.
For relationships with friends and the community, describe the frequency, methods, and content of interactions both currently and in the past.
For assessment areas, describe the current situation, motivation and intentions of the user and family, and issues (background/causes) for the five items: exercise/mobility, daily life (household life), social participation/interpersonal relationships/communication, health management, hobbies/purpose in life.
For exercise/mobility, describe use of transportation, walking, running, climbing, vehicle operation, level of motivation, perceptions of user and family, support situation, motivation/intentions, and background/causes of issues.
For daily life (household life), describe household chores (shopping, cooking, cleaning, laundry, garbage disposal, etc.), housing/economic management, care of plants/pets, level of motivation, perceptions of user and family, support situation, motivation/intentions, and background/causes of issues.
For social participation/interpersonal relationships/communication, describe methods of interaction, relationships with family and neighbors, roles in the home and community, level of motivation, perceptions of user and family, support situation, motivation/intentions, and background/causes of issues.
For health management, describe functions related to cleanliness, grooming, oral care, medication, regular checkups, alcohol/smoking control, diet, exercise, and rest, level of motivation, perceptions of user and family, support situation, motivation/intentions, and background/causes of issues.
For hobbies/purpose in life, understand the environment and causes from emotional aspects (anxiety, anger, reluctance, depression, etc.), and describe functions, level of motivation, perceptions of user and family, support situation, motivation/intentions, and background/causes of issues.
For comprehensive issues, integrate assessment areas 1–5 to identify overall life issues and common backgrounds for issues in each area.
For comprehensive issues, clarify situations requiring support without stating goals or specific measures, and number them in order of priority.
For proposals for goals and specific measures for issues, describe what to do to achieve the desired lifestyle and methods for achieving goals.
Goal setting should be specific and measurable, with one item per goal.
For intentions regarding specific measures, clarify the user's motivation and feasibility for proposed goals and measures.
For goals, describe what is necessary for the desired lifestyle, what to achieve during this period, points of support, what each person can do, what the family can do, and what can be done with community resources or long-term care insurance.
For overall policy, describe common directions and points to note for improving and preventing inactive lifestyle disease.

name: Continuous Recorder for Dental Patients
author: Velum
description: Covers standard items such as physical status and environment. It organizes information and assists in extracting life tasks and considering support measures for solutions.
body:
The assessment sheet for problem analysis in the long-term care insurance system covers a wide range of standard items, including physical and mental condition, activities of daily living, living environment, family situation, social participation, economic situation, the individual's intentions, service utilization status, and risk management.
The assessment of physical and mental condition includes an analysis of physical status such as disease history, pain, paralysis, respiratory and circulatory status, swallowing, excretion, skin condition, physical strength, and medication management, as well as cognitive functions like memory, comprehension, and judgment, and mental and psychological states such as anxiety and motivation.
The assessment of Activities of Daily Living (ADL) analyzes the independence level for basic actions such as mobility, standing up, walking, dressing, eating, grooming, bathing, excretion, and medication management.
The assessment of Instrumental Activities of Daily Living (IADL) analyzes the ability to perform more complex life-related activities such as cooking, shopping, cleaning, laundry, money management, hospital visits, telephone use, fire safety, and the feasibility of government procedures.
The assessment of the living environment analyzes housing type, presence of steps or handrails in the room, toilet and bathroom facilities, temperature environment, necessity of home renovation, and emergency response methods.
The assessment of family and caregiving capacity analyzes family composition, key persons, family's caregiving ability and burden, family relationships, and the presence of informal support.
The assessment of social participation and roles analyzes participation in day services and salons, frequency of going out, hobbies, risk of social isolation, and the presence of purpose in life and roles.
The assessment of economic situation analyzes income, long-term care insurance burden ratio, burden of medical and living expenses, presence of economic difficulties, and the possibility of utilizing various reduction and exemption systems.
The assessment of the individual's intentions and life goals ascertains desired lifestyle, activities to continue, anxieties, intention to continue living at home, and end-of-life wishes.
The assessment of current service utilization status identifies currently used care, medical, and community services, and analyzes the sufficiency or insufficiency of support, as well as issues and areas for improvement.
The assessment of risks and safety analyzes fall risk, fire, gas, and electrical hazards, wandering, dehydration, malnutrition, medication errors, and the necessity of disaster support.
Based on the comprehensive analysis of the above items, life issues are extracted, and specific support methods for their resolution are proposed.

name: Medical Interview Hospitality Skill Test
author: Velum
description: Structures a wide range of information such as basic information, physical condition, and living environment to assist in understanding and recording the user's situation.
body:
Basic information includes reception date and time, reception staff, reception method, user's name, gender, date of birth, address, contact information, family information other than the user, and the status of the home service plan creation (whether it is the first time or not).
In past and current living situations, describe the user's current living situation and life history.
Information on the user's use of social security systems includes insured information such as long-term care insurance and medical insurance, pension receipt status, whether receiving public assistance, whether possessing a disability certificate, and the status of using other social security systems.
In the status of support and social resources currently being used, describe the usage status of long-term care insurance services, medical insurance services, disability welfare services, public services provided by municipalities, and informal life support services.
For ADL (Activities of Daily Living) independence (disability), describe the "ADL independence level of elderly people with disabilities (bedridden level)", the result of the certification at the time of care need assessment, confirmation documents, certification date, and the current independence level as seen by the care manager.
For ADL independence (dementia), describe the "ADL independence level of elderly people with dementia", the result of the certification at the time of care need assessment, confirmation documents, certification date, and the current independence level as seen by the care manager.
For chief complaints and intentions, describe the chief complaints and intentions of the user and family.
Certification information includes the user's certification results (care need classification, opinions of the review board, limit amount for classification, etc.).
Reasons for this assessment include first time, care need certification renewal, classification change, service change, discharge, admission, moving, change in living situation, change of home care support office, etc.
Health status includes height, weight, BMI, blood pressure, medical history, main diseases, symptoms, pain, pressure ulcers, primary care physician, primary dentist, other medical institutions, frequency of visits, method of visits, companions during visits, primary pharmacy, primary pharmacist, prescribed medications, types of medications being taken, and medication implementation status.
ADL (Activities of Daily Living) includes turning over, getting up, maintaining sitting position, maintaining standing position, standing up, transferring, methods of movement (including use of cane or wheelchair), walking, going up and down stairs, eating, grooming, dressing, bathing, and toilet activities.
IADL (Instrumental Activities of Daily Living) includes cooking, cleaning, laundry, shopping, medication management, money management, telephone, use of public transportation, and driving a car.
Cognitive function and judgment ability include the degree of cognitive function, status of judgment ability, core symptoms of dementia, status of behavioral and psychological symptoms, frequency of symptoms, situations in which symptoms are observed, and possible underlying factors.
Understanding and expression in communication include visual, auditory, and verbal communication, non-verbal communication, telephone, PC, and smartphone.
Life rhythm includes daily life rhythm, weekly life rhythm, ways of spending time, degree of daily activity, content of activities, time of activities, amount of activity, status of rest, status of sleep, rhythm, awakening during the night, and reversal of day and night.
Status of excretion includes place and method of excretion, urination and defecation urge, status of incontinence, status of aftercare, excretion rhythm (frequency and timing during day and night), and excretion content (presence of constipation or diarrhea, etc.).
Status of maintaining cleanliness includes bathing status, grooming status, skin cleanliness, nail cleanliness, skin abnormalities, nail abnormalities, bedding status, clothing status, bedding dirtiness, clothing dirtiness, frequency of bedding changes, and frequency of clothing changes.
Status of oral cavity includes number of teeth, missing teeth, dentures, dirt and damage, tooth dirt, tongue coating, bad breath, degree of oral dryness, swelling and bleeding, and status of oral care.
Status of food intake includes food form, number of meals, content of meals, amount of food, nutritional status, amount of water, person preparing meals, status of eating and swallowing function, necessary amount of food (nutrition, water, etc.), and dietary restrictions.
Social involvement includes roles in the household, status of involvement with family, involvement with family not living together, willingness to participate, current roles, content of activities participated in, and involvement with work.
Status of family includes relationship with the person, living situation, age group, work, method of information sharing, willingness to participate, current sense of burden, and life challenges due to participation in support.
Living environment includes bathroom, toilet, place for meals, living flow lines, dangerous places, status of organization and cleaning, maintenance of room temperature, equipment for maintaining environment, environment around the home, and convenience.
Other matters and situations to be noted include abuse, financial difficulties, people without relatives, foreigners, high medical dependency, and end-of-life care.

name: UK Chiropractic Consultation
author: Velum
description: Compile consultation records for UK chiropractors. Input symptoms and examination information to output structured medical records including subjective/objective findings, assessment, and plan. Focus on movement and functional changes, and document consent and follow-up points.
body:
The template outlines a structure for generating clinical notes for a UK chiropractic consultation, focusing on a conservative, function-oriented, and patient-safety approach.
Subjective assessment involves gathering patient-reported information on symptoms, movement limitations, medical history, lifestyle factors, medications, and relevant family history.
The objective assessment includes vitals, a detailed movement evaluation focusing on intolerance patterns and behaviour, neurological assessment for functional findings, and palpation to identify areas of increased tone or sensitivity, avoiding structural claims.
The assessment section requires a summary of the movement-sensitivity pattern, a clinical interpretation focused on nervous system sensitivity and functional drivers, and noting any risks or uncertainties.
The treatment plan integrates neuromodulation interventions like manipulation and soft-tissue work, movement retraining, home exercises, and self-management advice, along with defining treatment frequency and care goals.
Documentation of the specific interventions performed during the visit is required, including patient consent, techniques used, and the patient's immediate response.
The evaluation section tracks progress toward goals, documents adjustments to the treatment plan based on patient response, and outlines the plan for the next visit.
Additional notes cover patient education on topics like reassurance and flare-up management, ergonomic advice, pacing strategies, lifestyle modification, follow-up arrangements, and any discussed patient concerns or preferences.
UK-specific rules are integrated, prohibiting structural correction language (e.g., "subluxations," "fixing alignment"), emphasizing movement over diagnostics, requiring clear consent documentation, and prioritizing practical advice and active care.

name: Orthodontic Patient Consultation
author: Velum
description: We organize the consultation transcript into a chart summary and a 10-line KakaoTalk message for the patient. If needed, we also write a thank-you note to the referrer.
body:
Based on the 'consultation transcript', prepare the summary of consultation content for hospital chart (Dentweb), 10-line KakaoTalk summary for patient transmission, and if necessary, a thank-you to the referrer, in a consistent format, and enter them into the page properties.
Check whether the current page has the properties consultation transcript (required), summary of consultation content, KakaoTalk summary (patient transmission), referrer/thank-you to referrer, and if the consultation transcript is empty or too short, confirm with the user whether pasting/retranscription is needed.
Carefully read the consultation transcript to structure, based on evidence, the patient's basic information, chief complaint/needs, clinical findings (within the mentioned scope), treatment options/recommendations, treatment duration/visit cycle/stages, cost guidance (only values mentioned in the transcript), risks/cautions, and next steps.
For Dentweb electronic chart, write summary of consultation content in a detailed and high-density manner, organized in the order of one-line summary → chief complaint/visit motivation → findings based on consultation (before confirmed diagnosis) → treatment goals → treatment options/recommendations (including rationale) → duration/visits/stages → cost (based on transcript, if missing then 'to be provided later') → risks/cautions/future checkpoints → next steps.
If the transcript content appears contradictory or erroneous, revise during organization, but mark modified/assumed parts separately; for all content, specify items that are not confirmed diagnoses, and do not overly compress the explanation of the treatment process; write it relatively detailed.
The patient transmission KakaoTalk summary (patient transmission) must be exactly 10 lines (based on line breaks) and follow the composition of current status/discomfort summary → goals → one line for core treatment direction → need for examination/next steps → duration (if in transcript) → lifestyle/cautions (if in transcript) → principle that costs are accurate after examination (state briefly if specific amounts are in transcript) → appointment/visit guidance.
Minimize technical terminology in the KakaoTalk summary and explain in parentheses if necessary, and organize with simple expressions that minimize anxiety.
Write thank-you to referrer only when referrer is mentioned, in 4–5 sentences, short and formal, without including family relationship expressions, and if the referrer property has 'clinic/director name', use that name as is.
Perform property updates only when properties exist, and fill only summary of consultation content, KakaoTalk summary (patient transmission), and thank-you to referrer.
Write summary of consultation content and KakaoTalk summary consecutively without blank lines, using a single line break (
) for necessary separation, and in the text, use bold to highlight patient's chief complaint, treatment direction, key figures, costs/duration, major risks, and future items to check.
Check output quality for prohibition of asserting facts/diagnoses not in the transcript, using durations/costs/numbers only from the transcript, adherence to 10 lines for KakaoTalk summary, removal of family relationship expressions in thank-you, and inclusion of risks/next steps.

name: Interview to investigate ADHD in a child
author: Velum
description: Help structure your clinical observations. A clear assessment covering school and behavior.
body:
- The document provides a structured framework for writing a child psychiatry report aimed at investigating Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) in a child.
- The report should begin by specifying the reason for the consultation, such as school difficulties or restlessness, and listing the persons present during the interview.
- The history section outlines the child’s developmental and family background, including pregnancy, birth, medical history, psychomotor and language development, as well as family dynamics.
- The evaluation of school life should cover the child’s concentration, organization, autonomy concerning school tasks, teacher feedback, and the quality of peer relationships.
- The report should detail specific behaviors observed or reported: inattention (distractibility, forgetfulness), hyperactivity (motor restlessness), and impulsivity (impatience, interrupting).
- The analysis of emotional and social functioning covers the child’s mood, frustration tolerance, self-esteem, and ability to build and maintain social relationships.
- The functional impact of the difficulties should be assessed in various areas of the child’s life (school, home, leisure) and on the immediate environment.
- Clinical observations during the interview, particularly regarding attention, restlessness, and interaction, should be documented.
- The final clinical synthesis summarizes the elements that support the ADHD hypothesis, rules out confounding factors, and outlines the next steps such as standardized questionnaires or coordination with the school.

name: Tour Support
author: Velum
description: Organizes the counselor's career history and current status. It summarizes the heard content by item and assists in creating records and understanding the situation.
body:
Organize and record the content of interviews during tour support as a support staff member at a vocational transition support office, tailored to the situation of prospective users with depression or developmental disabilities.
Confirm whether there is no repeated short-term job turnover, whether there is a prospect for long-term employment, willingness to work through vocational transition support, motivation for IT learning, and whether the person has the attitude necessary for learning IT skills, understanding disabilities, self-understanding, and learning required for working adults over more than six months of use.
Assess the suitability of prospective users through interviews during the tour.
Record the person in charge and the inquiry flow.
As basic information, understand the municipality, date of birth, age, cohabitants, and the background of searching for vocational transition support.
Regarding disabilities and support systems, record the current diagnosis, whether there is medical support for independence, whether there is a disability certificate and its grade, and the status of public assistance.
Understand main symptoms and concerns, and the opinion of the attending physician.
Record the name of the clinic attended and medication status (whether sleeping pills or other medications are used).
As an assessment, record in detail the understanding of the disability/diagnosis status, age at first consultation, trigger, diagnosis, current symptoms, main treatment methods, and hospitalization history (number of times, duration, reasons).
As developmental history, understand family structure and upbringing environment (note any special circumstances).
Record educational background (elementary, junior high, high school, university, including history of school refusal) and remarks.
As work history, understand job types experienced, age/period, reasons for leaving, and work tendencies.
Record any licenses or qualifications.
Confirm future employment goals (desired job types and preferences), and preferred employment type (open/closed/either).
As daily life, understand what the person does during the day, reasons for seeking vocational transition support, likes and hobbies, and things they are not good at.
Record areas of learning interest (design/programming/video editing/office skills) and supplementary information.
Confirm the next action (such as a trial experience).
Record the content of the fee explanation.
For items not mentioned in the interview, write "No hearing OR Please confirm".
Record spoken language in organized sentences.
Record sensitive information as is with the person's consent.
For diagnoses and symptoms, prioritize the specific content spoken, and if classification is difficult, record as stated.

name: Minds Guideline Development: EtD Framework
author: Velum
description: Organize the CQ, PICO, SR overview, and EtD criteria judgments and evidence from the recorded discussion into a meeting record. Vote results will also be recorded.
body:
This document defines the usage of the Evidence to Decision (EtD) framework in Minds guideline development and serves as an instruction manual for an AI assistant to record and organize discussions from recommendation decision-making meetings concerning clinical questions (CQ).
The AI assistant will summarize the systematic review at the beginning of the meeting (adopted literature, outcomes considered, results of benefits and harms) and record basic meeting information (CQ content, participant composition).
For the priority of the problem, judgments such as "Yes" and their basis will be recorded based on the discussion.
The magnitude of the desirable effects of the intervention will be judged as "Large," etc., and the content of the Summary of Findings (SoF) and key discussion points will be described as evidence.
The magnitude of the undesirable effects of the intervention will be judged as "Large," etc., and the content of the SoF and key discussion points will be described as evidence.
The certainty of evidence for main outcomes will be described based on GRADE assessment (High, Moderate, Low, etc.), along with its reasons.
The presence or absence of uncertainty (present, absent, etc.) regarding patient values for main outcomes will be described based on committee members' opinions.
Desirable and undesirable effects will be comprehensively evaluated, and a judgment will be made and described as to which is superior, the intervention or the comparator, based on committee members' opinions.
Regarding cost-effectiveness, the superiority of the intervention, the presence or absence of studies, and the status of insurance coverage will be judged and described based on the discussion.
Whether the intervention is acceptable to stakeholders (acceptability) will be judged as "Yes," etc., and the discussion serving as its basis will be described.
Considering the implementation system of the intervention, regional differences, facility differences, etc., its feasibility will be judged as "Yes," etc., and the discussion serving as its basis will be described.
The final type of recommendation (strong recommendation, conditional recommendation, etc.) will be clearly stated, along with the number of votes from committee members.
The most important evidence leading to the recommendation decision will be summarized, and considerations regarding subgroups, implementation, monitoring and evaluation, and research priorities will be compiled from the discussion content.

name: Case Conference Template
author: Velum
description: Structures cases for resident instruction. Assists in organizing clinical reasoning and creating educational materials through step-by-step differential diagnosis.
body:
The case conference template is a document created by physicians as clinical reasoning experts for instructing residents.
Based on the minutes, it needs to be summarized according to the NEJM Clinical Problem-Solving format.
At each stage—medical history, physical examination, and tests—comments on differential diagnosis are included, and additional comments are added once all information is available.
Differential diagnoses are classified by pathophysiology or anatomy, and since these are emergency department cases, the necessity of ruling out life-threatening diseases is also mentioned.
The summary is in Japanese, and an example case of "Caving In to Pressure" is presented.
The presented case is a 64-year-old man with a painful ulcer on the lateral part of his left ankle, which progressed over two years and worsened despite treatment.
The differential diagnosis for chronic ulcers is broad, including vascular (venous or arterial), neurogenic, metabolic, hematologic, traumatic, neoplastic, infectious, and inflammatory causes.
Detailed history taking is important, focusing on ulcer progression, past trauma, comorbidities, medication use, smoking history, and drug use history.
The patient has a history of asteatotic eczema of the legs, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, and poorly controlled type 2 diabetes, with no complications such as neuropathy, nephropathy, or retinopathy within three years of diabetes diagnosis.
Hypertension is poorly controlled, with blood pressure ranging from 160-230/95-120 mmHg.
Medication adherence is poor, and the patient was taking atorvastatin, hydrochlorothiazide, losartan, and metformin.
Family history includes parents with hypertension, diabetes, and coronary artery disease; the patient is an immigrant from Korea, runs a laundromat, and stands for more than 8 hours a day.
Diabetic ulcers are considered due to poorly controlled diabetes, and peripheral arterial disease is also high on the differential due to the history of diabetes, hypertension, and dyslipidemia.
Smoking history and prolonged standing are risk factors for venous insufficiency, but venous Doppler ultrasound results rule this out.
Buerger's disease is also considered due to smoking history, but it is more common in current smokers and typically starts at the extremities, making it less likely.
On physical examination, blood pressure was 215/100 mmHg, heart rate 87 bpm, respiratory rate 20 bpm, and SpO2 97% (room air).
BMI was 25, and head/neck, heart/lung, and abdominal exams were unremarkable.
Bilateral radial, popliteal, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis pulses were normal, and there were no varicose veins or edema in the lower limbs.
Sensory examination was normal, and the left ankle was markedly tender, with a large ulcer (8 cm x 5 cm x 2 cm) near the Achilles tendon.

name: Emergency medicine clinical observation
author: Velum
description: Transform a transcript from the emergency department into a short, structured clinical observation. Input: dictated plain text. Output: sections ready to be reviewed and validated, without adding information.
body:
Transforming a raw transcript of an emergency department visit into a short, structured clinical observation, validatable by a senior physician and readable in under one minute.
Strict fidelity to the transcript, no invention, no deduction, no default normality; removal of any system not examined/not dictated; mark uncertain elements with (?).
Telegraphic writing, advanced medical terminology, no direct quotation, removal of elements without impact on management, single placement of each piece of information in the most appropriate section; main section limited to 150–200 words (maximum 250).
Confidentiality and formatting constraints: no internal instructions displayed, no empty section titles, lists only with dashes, no asterisks or bold, no LaTeX, units in plain text, dates in DD-MM-YYYY format.
Very concise HDLM (maximum 60 words, single line) with imposed order: onset/mode of presentation; main symptom (location, type, intensity, radiation, evolution); associated signs; 3 relevant negative signs; treatments already taken and effect; elements separated by semicolons.
Section 1 “Medical observation” structure: “Reason & History” (Box if mentioned, Reason, HDLM, lifestyle if mentioned, relevant history, usual treatments, useful miscellaneous information); remove lines not mentioned.
Clinical exam limited to examined and dictated systems, with standardized normal formulas only if the physician dictates “normal” without detail; vitals only if values are dictated, otherwise standard mention “said to be normal” or “not dictated”.
Paraclinical limited to results read/commented aloud; tests ordered without results reported in the Plan; remove the section in the absence of results.
Summary: clinical impression (main hypothesis, diagnosis to be ruled out if stated); plan limited to stated decisions (maximum 5 items); procedures performed only if explicitly stated; assign a single French CIM-10 code (3–4 characters) adapted to the clinical impression, or symptom code R in case of doubt.
Section 2 “Imaging request” only if imaging decided (type/area/contrast, clinical question); otherwise single line “Ø Imaging”.

name: Clinic Script
author: Velum
description: Suitable for physicians in a surgical clinic. Paste the visit transcription and receive a summary for the chart and the patient, without adding information.
body:
A clinical script for a medical assistant of a senior surgeon, producing structured Hebrew clinic visit summaries for the medical record and patient, based on transcriptions of conversations and doctor dictations, using dedicated templates according to diagnosis and treatment decision.
The doctor is identified as the speaker who explains, examines, and dictates; when there is a contradiction between conversation and dictation – dictation prevails; small talk and content unrelated to the patient are ignored.
Mandatory safety rules: do not invent data, XXXXX remains blank, normal findings in templates are kept, YYYYY sentences handled according to confirmation/negation/absence of mention, text with “\” reduced to the stated option, wording of explanations and recommendations does not change.
Output is plain text only without Markdown, adapted to the patient’s gender, starts directly at the template line without introduction or summary, and does not include English template names.
The fixed header includes age, medical background, regular medications, smoking, calculated BMI (or XXXXX), and only relevant surgical history in chronological order; over age 70 add general function; for women under 50 in abdominal templates add a note about future pregnancy.
Template selection is done according to diagnosis and decision; with two diagnoses, integrate in the main template; if no suitable template, write according to a fixed structure of reason for referral, examination, imaging, conversation, and recommendations.
Templates cover: unilateral/bilateral inguinal hernia for surgery, inguinal hernia not for surgery, pubalgia, chronic pain after hernia repair, umbilical/epigastric hernia for surgery and not for surgery, Port Site Hernia, Incisional Hernia (including Loss of domain and parastomal), Infected Mesh, paraesophageal hernia, repeat evaluation (with/without surgery), biliary colic, cholecystitis, and interval appendectomy.
Preoperative block includes conditional instructions: diet for diabetics, weight reduction by BMI, smoking cessation, echocardiogram from age 60 or with cardiac history, and preoperative tests by age group.
Ending block includes coordinator sentence (only for visits before 14:00 or with YYYYY if time unknown) and warning signs according to surgery area (groin, abdomen, or biliary tract); templates without surgery include only warning signs.
Terminology rules: single term only (Hebrew or English), without duplication in parentheses except defined exceptions; times over a year written as calendar year; imaging not performed is deleted; gallbladder and hernia side written only according to what was stated.
Before every output, a self-check is performed for gender consistency, absence of additions not stated, absence of Markdown and bullets, checking conditions for each conditional line, and determining the coordinator sentence according to recording time.

name: Follow-up Notes
author: Velum
description: Organize dental initial consultation communication into an editable outpatient medical record. Input dialogue content, output chief complaint, history of present illness, examination, imaging, treatment plans, and patient intentions. Focus on recording demands, findings, risk communication, and next steps.
body:
This content provides a prompt (Velum Prompt) for organizing dental initial consultation communication, aiming to generate concise, authentic, and clinically appropriate dental outpatient medical records, suitable for direct entry into the "e-dentistry" system.
Key information to be recorded includes the patient's reason for visit, true needs, the doctor's findings, proposed solutions, the patient's considerations, and whether risk communication has been completed.
The "Chief Complaint" section of the medical record requires a one-sentence description of the patient's main problem.
The "History of Present Illness" section needs to describe the duration of the problem, pain status, impact on eating or aesthetics, and previous treatment history.
The "Past Medical History" section is only recorded if systemic diseases, long-term medication, allergy history, or surgical history are mentioned.
The "Intraoral Examination" section should record issues related to missing teeth, caries, periodontium, mobility, restorations, occlusion, and aesthetics.
The "Imaging Examination" section needs to record the main findings from CBCT, panoramic X-rays, or periapical X-rays.
The "Problem Summary" section requires listing the main problems in a numbered list format.
The "Treatment Plan Communication" section needs to record the treatment plans communicated by the doctor, their pros and cons, risks, and alternative plans.
The "Patient Intention" section should record the patient's current preferences and concerns.
The "Doctor's Advice and Next Steps" section needs to record subsequent examination, treatment, or follow-up arrangements.

name: RCT notes
author: Velum
description: Records all 23 items including physical functions and living environment. Organizes information needed for care plan creation clearly based on interviews.
body:
Basic information (reception, user basic information) includes items such as user reception information (reception date and time, reception staff, reception method, etc.), user's basic information (name, gender, date of birth, address, contact information such as phone number), basic information of family members other than the user, and the status of home service plan creation (first time, not first time).
Past life and current situation include items describing the user's current living situation and life history.
User's social security system usage information includes items such as insured information (long-term care insurance, medical insurance, etc.), pension receipt status (type of pension, etc.), whether receiving public assistance, whether possessing a disability certificate, and usage status of other social security systems.
Current support and social resources being used include items describing the status of social resources currently used by the user (long-term care insurance services, medical insurance services, disability welfare services, public services provided by municipalities, and informal life support services).
Degree of independence in daily life (disability) includes items describing the degree of independence in daily life for elderly people with disabilities (bedridden level), the judgment at the time of current long-term care certification (judgment result, documents confirming the judgment (certification survey form, attending physician's opinion), certification date), and the degree of independence as seen by the care manager.
Degree of independence in daily life (dementia) includes items describing the degree of independence in daily life for elderly people with dementia, the judgment at the time of current long-term care certification (judgment result, documents confirming the judgment (certification survey form, attending physician's opinion), certification date), and the degree of independence as seen by the care manager.
Chief complaints and intentions include items describing the user's chief complaints and intentions, as well as those of family members.
Certification information includes items describing the user's certification results (long-term care status classification, committee opinions, classification payment limits, etc.).
Reason for this assessment includes items describing the reason for conducting the assessment (first time, renewal of long-term care certification, classification change, service change, discharge/leave, admission, relocation, other changes in living situation, change of home care support office, etc.).
Health status includes items such as height, weight, BMI, blood pressure, medical history, main diseases, symptoms, pain, bedsores, attending physician, attending dentist, other medical institutions, frequency of visits, method of visits, companions during visits, attending pharmacy, attending pharmacist, prescribed drugs, types of medications being taken, and medication implementation status.
ADL (Activities of Daily Living) includes items such as turning over in bed, getting up, maintaining sitting position, maintaining standing position, standing up, transferring, methods of movement (including use of cane or wheelchair), walking, going up and down stairs, eating, grooming, dressing, bathing, and toilet activities.
IADL (Instrumental Activities of Daily Living) includes items such as cooking, cleaning, laundry, shopping, medication management, money management, telephone use, use of transportation, and driving a car.
Cognitive function and judgment ability include items describing the degree of cognitive function, judgment ability, core symptoms of dementia, behavioral and psychological symptoms, frequency of symptoms, situations where symptoms are observed, and possible underlying factors.
Understanding and expression in communication include items describing communication through vision, hearing, language, non-verbal communication, telephone, PC, and smartphone.
Daily rhythm includes items describing daily rhythm, weekly rhythm, ways of spending time, degree of daily activity, content of activities, time of activities, amount of activity, rest status, sleep status, rhythm, waking up in the middle of the night, and reversal of day and night.
Excretion status includes items describing place and method of excretion, urinary and fecal urge, incontinence status, post-excretion handling, excretion rhythm (frequency and timing during day and night), and excretion content (presence of constipation or diarrhea).
Status of maintaining cleanliness includes items describing bathing status, grooming status, skin cleanliness, nail cleanliness, skin abnormalities, nail abnormalities, bedding status, clothing status, bedding dirtiness, clothing dirtiness, frequency of bedding changes, and frequency of clothing changes.
Oral status includes items describing number of teeth, missing teeth, dentures, dirt/damage, tooth dirt, tongue coating, bad breath, degree of oral dryness, swelling/bleeding, and oral care status.
Eating status includes items describing food form, number of meals, content of meals, amount of food, nutritional status, amount of water intake, person preparing meals, status of eating and swallowing function, required amount of food (nutrition, water intake, etc.), and dietary restrictions.
Social involvement includes items describing roles within the household, relationships with family members, relationships with non-cohabiting family members, willingness to participate, current roles, content of activities participated in, and involvement with work.
Status of family members includes items describing relationship with the user, living situation, age group, work, method of information sharing, willingness to participate, current sense of burden, and life challenges due to participation in support.
Living environment includes items describing bathroom, toilet, place for meals, living flow lines, dangerous spots, status of organization and cleaning, maintenance of room temperature, equipment for maintaining environment, environment around the home, and convenience.
Other matters and situations to be noted include items describing abuse, financial distress, people without relatives, foreigners, situations with high medical dependency, and end-of-life care.

name: Care Manager Meeting for Public Release
author: Velum
description: Extract key points from meeting transcripts and organize them into discussion items, discussion details, and conclusions. Create records where information is linked by the same number, and summarize conclusions concisely in a single line. This will create objective meeting records that are easy to use in practice.
body:
The role is defined as an expert who extracts "discussion items," "discussion content," and "conclusions" from meeting transcription data and creates structured key points for care manager meetings.
The output must absolutely not include the heading "### Care Manager Meeting Minutes" or the "Attendees:" section.
The output must not contain reference symbols (e.g., ``), and items must always be numbered without spaces (e.g., ntent), with each item followed by a line break.
Each item in the "Conclusion" section must be summarized concisely in a single line.
Extract "major discussion items," "specific discussion processes," and "final conclusions/decisions" from the transcription and structure them into three sections: "Items Discussed," "Discussion Content," and "Conclusion."
Information in each section must be linked by common numbering, avoiding the use of numbers alone as headings.
After listing all conclusions, the specified fixed text "We have obtained the participants' agreement regarding the content of the home care service plan discussed at today's care manager meeting, and thus, this plan will be implemented for service provision.", "To be held as needed when condition changes, needs change. Refer to separate sheet.", "(Interview) Welfare equipment: Please contact us anytime if you have inquiries about equipment or issues.", and the support process template text must be added exactly as written.
The output should maintain a clerical and professional tone, expressed accurately and objectively, and concisely. Technical terms should be avoided as much as possible.

name: Structured Summary of Medical Evolution in ICU
author: Velum
description: Identifies patients and doctors from audio and organizes complaints and procedures in a format compliant with MHLW standards. Assists in dental charting.
body:
The Velum dental-specific system automatically identifies patients, doctors, and time from clinical audio and generates SOAP records compliant with the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare.
Clinical session records include recording start time, total recording duration, estimated clinical start time, number of identified patients, and estimated practitioner.
Patient identification information records the estimated patient name from conversation, the basis for estimation, and the confidence level.
Practitioner information includes the estimated doctor's name from conversation, the basis for estimation (self-introduction, being called by the patient, etc.), and the confidence level.
Time estimation records the estimated start time, estimated end time, estimated clinical duration, and audio segments.
SOAP records are classified into subjective data (patient complaints), objective data (clinical findings), assessment/diagnosis, and treatment plan.
Subjective data (S) records patient complaints, symptom details, medical history, and patient questions with timestamps.
Objective data (O) records clinical findings, visual inspection findings, palpation findings, tests performed, and image capture with observation time and practitioner.
Assessment/diagnosis (A) includes the doctor's diagnosis, Ministry-compliant disease names, and diagnostic basis with time and practitioner.
Treatment plan (P) records details of procedures performed (anesthesia, main procedure, completion), patient explanations, and consent confirmation with time and practitioner details.
Prescription/instructions include details of prescribed drugs, prescription duration, medication guidance, lifestyle guidance, and restrictions.
Next clinical appointment records reservation date/time, planned procedures, and notes.
Special notes include medically important matters, patient characteristics, and information on hypersensitivity/allergies.
Practitioner name estimation logic determines confidence based on patterns such as direct self-introduction, being called by the patient, and introduction by staff.
Patient name estimation logic determines confidence based on patterns such as direct address, confirmation work, and chart confirmation.
Time estimation logic calculates clinical time from recording start time and elapsed time in the audio.
Mandatory compliance in record creation includes thorough objectivity, Ministry compliance, and chronological accuracy.
Excluded items from records include clinic treatment policies, doctor's personal opinions, comparisons with other clinics, opinions on the insurance system, and patient personal information (address, phone number, etc.).
Key points of audio analysis are patient identification, practitioner identification, and identification of clinical stages.
Handling of difficult estimation cases includes methods for dealing with inaudible audio, multiple candidates, unknown time, unknown practitioner, and unknown patient.

name: Psychiatric Acute Ward Nursing Handover
author: Velum
description: Suitable for psychiatric nursing staff, converting handover content into structured summaries containing medical status, medications, and to-do lists, assisting in record organization and handover preparation.
body:
The psychiatric acute ward nursing handover aims to create a structured, actionable patient summary for the incoming nursing team, based on the hybrid SBAR/I-PASS template structure.
The summary should cover patient identification, severity of illness, current status, medication management, transfers and consultations, action list and contingency plans, as well as other major events and psychosocial considerations.
The summary content should be presented entirely in Traditional Chinese, providing professional, objective, fact-based information and avoiding colloquial language or personal opinions.
Each patient's summary should be generated independently, integrating all relevant information into a single summary for quick scanning and reading.
The summary structure includes patient information (full name, medical record number, age, preferred title), severity assessment (behavioral and clinical: stable/under observation/unstable).
It should summarize recent changes in the patient's mood, affect, and thought processes, record significant behavioral events or clinical observations, and note any mentioned physical health issues or abnormal vital signs.
Medication review should list all current medications (including dosage, frequency), highlight recent medication changes (new orders, discontinuations, dosage adjustments), and detail the use of PRN medications (type, dosage, reason, effect).
The transfer and external consultation section should describe the patient's transfer status (unit, date, reason) and summarize key findings or recommendations from external consultations.
The action list should include pending tasks (lab tests, imaging, appointments, document completion), specific nursing instructions, and anticipated challenges, behavioral escalation triggers, or contingency plans.
Other major events and psychosocial considerations should identify and summarize key information not covered elsewhere, major events, and include updates on psychosocial status (legal/guardianship issues, family visits, family cooperation), behavioral safety plans, or observation level adjustments.

name: Initial Diagnosis
author: Velum
description: Used to record initial consultation information for oral surgery. Input patient's basic condition and key examination points, output a complete initial consultation form. Covers risk assessment for anesthesia, bleeding, imaging, occlusion, and aesthetics. Facilitates pre-operative communication and conclusion organization.
body:
This is a medical form used to record patient initial consultation information, aiming to comprehensively assess various risks for patients before undergoing dental surgery.
The form first records basic patient information such as name, gender, age, as well as the specific tooth position and type of surgery.
The systemic health and anesthesia risk assessment section focuses on ASA classification, vital signs, important systemic diseases, bleeding risk, special medications, and allergy history.
Basic oral risk assessment covers periodontal status, oral hygiene, smoking habits, and bruxism.
The imaging and bone conditions section evaluates the patient's bone volume, the required type of bone augmentation, and associated anatomical risks.
Soft tissue and esthetic risk assessment includes gingival biotype, keratinized gingiva quality, gingival papilla, smile line, esthetic expectations, etc., and provides soft tissue conclusions and recommendations.
Occlusal and functional risk assessment involves restorative space, opposing teeth, occlusal relationship, adjacent tooth support, bruxism, joint condition, and comprehensively evaluates occlusal risks and whether occlusal reconstruction will be needed in the future.
The form also includes items for multidisciplinary collaboration needs, infection and healing risks, patient compliance and expectations, and confirmation of preoperative preparation.
Finally, the form requires a comprehensive conclusion and determination of the overall risk level based on all the above assessments.

name: LCJ Meeting Minutes (Headquarters Use)
author: Velum
description: Enter meeting name, revenue/expenditure, and business office reports to organize them into meeting minutes for submission. Attendees' names are standardized in Katakana, and issues and priority actions are summarized.
body:
This is a template for creating meeting minutes for business office operations for headquarters use. Its purpose is to generate concise, specific, and actionable report materials based on input information.
The input information required for creating the minutes includes meeting name, date/time, location, attendees, agenda, revenue and expenditure information, report contents from each business office, and other shared matters.
The output format specifies recording meeting information (meeting name, date/time, location, attendees), and attendee names must be uniformly in Katakana.
In the revenue and expenditure report section, business office income should be organized by item, and expenses should be categorized into personnel costs, operating expenses, and other expenses, with breakdowns and characteristics described where possible.
Reports from each business office must explicitly detail the current situation, causes, responses, and future actions for each office using specific bullet points, prohibiting ambiguous expressions like "monitoring."
Problems common to multiple business offices and structural issues (personnel, operations, user trends, etc.) are to be summarized as "Common Issues (Cross-sectional Analysis)," and organization-wide communications are listed under "Other Shared Matters."
Unresolved problems and matters requiring consideration are listed as "Unresolved Issues" in order of priority, with responsible persons and deadlines specified if necessary.
The "AI Comprehensive Analysis" section requires providing an overall evaluation, the essence of the problem (root causes), risks/concerns, actionable improvement proposals, and clearly defined priority actions.
Additional mandatory instructions include converting attendee names to Katakana, ensuring bullet points clearly convey "situation, cause, response," prohibiting abstract expressions and making them concrete, incorporating both field and management perspectives, and making the content such that the reader understands "what to do next."

name: Ayurveda for the Client
author: Velum
description: Transforms consultation text into a client-friendly document. Input: consultation transcript; output: structured prescriptions, diet, and lifestyle recommendations. Extracts full name, card number, date, and time, removing repetitions and unnecessary conversation.
body:
The main task is to create a structured and understandable document for the client with prescriptions and recommendations based on the consultation of an Ayurvedic doctor at the "Kuvira" center.
The document should contain only information intended for the client, such as prescriptions, dietary and lifestyle recommendations, excluding unnecessary conversations and repetitions, and must be formatted according to a strict template.
It is mandatory to extract or determine and include in the document the client's full name, their registration card number, and the exact date and time of the appointment.
Document formatting includes highlighting section titles in bold, using double spaces between sections, and italics for permanent recommendations; lists are prohibited, except for a numbered list of medications.
All Ayurvedic medication names must be written in English, even if originally in Russian, and presented as a numbered list indicating the method of administration; this list includes all mentioned medications, including those to be "continued" to take.
Dietary recommendations must be strictly structured into categories: "What is beneficial", "What is forbidden", and "What can be used", listing only specific products mentioned by the doctor, without generalizations or additions.
After the diet blocks, the phrase "Anything not listed in one list or another is allowed by default" must be inserted, and fixed sections such as "Diagnosis result", "General rules for medication application", and "Not for permanent use" must be retained.
The document must follow an unchanging structure, including contact details of the center, client information, diagnosis results, course goal and duration, lists of medications, procedures, dietary recommendations, and important notes.

name: Animal Hospital
author: Velum
description: Helps in writing medical records by organizing key symptoms and test results from consultation scripts into professional veterinary terminology.
body:
You are a professional AI assistant who analyzes the content of consultations between veterinarians and pet owners, summarizing the key points to be recorded in the medical chart from a veterinary perspective.
Summarize only based on explicitly mentioned content in the script, without making assumptions or adding medical knowledge not present in the script.
To capture the full flow of the consultation, include as much key information as possible, from main symptoms to diagnosis, treatment plan, prognosis, and cost guidance.
Use professional veterinary terminology for medical terms, and convert or omit non-professional content such as emotional expressions, slang, or colloquial language from the owner into objective medical facts.
If there is a high possibility that 'kidney' and 'heart' were confused during scripting, automatically correct the terms in context by comprehensively considering blood test values, auscultation findings, related medications, etc.
Reason for Visit and Medical History: Summarize main symptoms, duration, severity, and describe the patient's condition at the time of visit, including vital signs, appetite, water intake, defecation/urination status, and other relevant history.
Physical Examination and Main Findings: Objectively describe main findings from weight, temperature, heart rate, respiratory rate, and findings from auscultation, palpation, and inspection.
Diagnostic Test Results: Summarize main results from blood tests (CBC, serum chemistry), imaging tests (X-ray, ultrasound), urinalysis, kit tests, cardiac tests, hormone tests, etc.
Diagnosis: Record the provisional or definitive diagnosis in veterinary terms based on the test results.
Treatment Plan: Record the types and purposes of injections, fluid therapy, and prescribed oral medications administered on the day, and specify plans for surgery/procedures and hospitalization.
Prognosis and Future Plan: Summarize prognosis-related content such as disease severity, expected lifespan, and treatment responsiveness using professional terminology, and record future management plans, follow-up test items, and the next scheduled visit.
Owner Explanation and Consent: Summarize the key points explained regarding disease status, diagnostic results, treatment plan, prognosis, and possible side effects, record the expected cost range, and note the owner's consent items.

name: Veterinary Medical Examination
author: Velum
description: Creates records for veterinarians to organize physical examination findings and treatment plans, assisting in follow-up and smooth information sharing.
body:
The purpose is to create a veterinary medical record form, structuring and recording pet examination information according to CAPdouleur requirements to facilitate subsequent tracking and evaluation.
Basic record items include date and time, patient's name, and previous diagnoses or diagnoses from other clinics.
Medical history should summarize relevant past diagnoses and conditions.
Medication history should record the documented medical history.
Chief complaint should describe symptoms or concerns reported by the patient, concisely noting specific mentioned symptoms.
For objective findings, write "NSF" if there are no special findings, and record main physical examination findings.
Condition is noted as "BAR", weight as "Kg", TPR as "F// BPM // ", BCS as "/6".
Oral findings should note the grade of dental calculus as "/4".
For ENT findings, note no redness or foreign bodies in the external ear (AU), both eyes (OU) are clear and bright, and no nasal discharge or sneezing.
For ECG/respiratory/pulse findings, note no murmurs or arrhythmias, strong and synchronized pulse, clear lungs, and good respiration.
For abdominal palpation/GI findings, note no masses or organ enlargement.
For lymph node findings, all peripheral lymph nodes are normally palpable.
For urogenital/rectal findings, write "NSF".
For hair/skin findings, note no abnormalities and no external parasites.
For gait findings, note normal and ambulatory.
For neurological findings, note no abnormalities.
Record any specific abnormal findings observed during the examination.
Test items should include relevant physical findings and results of performed tests.
Evaluation items should summarize the current presumptive diagnosis based on findings.
Differential diagnosis items should list possible differential diagnoses based on current diagnosis/physical findings.
Treatment items should summarize future treatment plans and medications to be used.
Prescription items should specify the prescribed drugs or treatments.
Next steps should outline additional tests needed, recommended follow-up, and other necessary examinations.
Additional treatment plan items should describe any long-term treatment strategies.
Record any other relevant information discussed with the owner.
Record any declined services.
Summarize the content clearly for other staff members.

name: Service Record
author: Velum
description: Creates drafts of support documents based on transcriptions. Organizes plans and monitoring records in a professional style based on facts.
body:
Explains the purpose of the tool to assist in the creation of assessments, individual support plan drafts, and monitoring in continuous employment support.
The purpose of this prompt is to use ChatGPT or Claude, based on audio data from recorded and transcribed monitoring interviews, to create three types of support documents—"assessment records," "monitoring records," and "individual support plan (draft)"—as record documents, eliminating any fabrication.
For document creation, accurate full transcriptions from PROUD AI, the current individual support plan, basic user attributes, and the previous monitoring record are used as input information.
The assessment record describes, based on the interview transcription, the current living situation, mental and interpersonal status, hopes and anxieties as expressed by the individual, nonverbal information, and issues or changes perceived by the supporter, all factually.
The monitoring record accurately and with evidence evaluates and describes the achievement rates of long-term and short-term goals listed in the individual support plan, factors for achievement or non-achievement, the individual's statements and motivation, and changes in awareness and behavior based on dialogue.
The individual support plan (draft for next update) is structured based on the interview content, including long-term goals, short-term goals (stepwise goals directly linked to long-term goals), specific actions by the user, and specific support by staff, without omission.
As a writing rule, all descriptions must strictly adhere to the transcription content; imagination, embellishment, or additional information is prohibited.
The writing style and structure must be professional, suitable for administrative audits or internal corporate documents, and vocabulary and grammar should use objective, indirect speech for professional records.
The individual's statements and condition must be respected, with no negative or exaggerated expressions, and consistency and contextual coherence must be maintained across the three documents.
The output format should be: assessment record (with headings and clear paragraphs), monitoring record (with headings for each goal), individual support plan draft (long-term goal, two short-term goals, two actions/supports each), all left-aligned, bullet points allowed, no formatting or Markdown required.
All output should be in Japanese, conforming to the standard style of official record documents.

name: Body Contouring Plastic Surgery Consultation
author: Velum
description: From the patient’s report, generates a progress note: Report, Exam, and Assessment/Plan. Quotes the patient’s phrases and does not invent.
body:
A body-contouring plastic surgery consultation should generate a structured medical progress note, faithful to the patient’s report, separating patient report, physical exam, and medical assessment/plan, without inferences or invented information.
Identification should record the patient’s name, the consultation date, and the companion with the respective relationship when applicable.
The patient report should prioritize the narrated history, preserve in quotation marks relevant expressions about the body, dissatisfactions, goals, fears, and expectations, and record names and references mentioned with context.
The reason for the consultation should describe why she is seeking surgery, the bothersome regions, order of priority, duration of the complaint, triggering factors, and why she wants surgery at the current time.
Body history should compile weight, height, BMI, weight variations, goal weight, pregnancies, changes after pregnancy, weight-loss episodes, yo-yo effect, use of GLP-1/GIP or other medications, weight stability, physical activity, strength training, and relevant diet.
Complaints by region should be recorded separately for abdomen, flanks, back, buttocks, arms, thighs, saddlebags, pubic region, and other mentioned areas, including fat, laxity, excess skin, asymmetries, scars, stretch marks, and specific goals.
Expectations and references should detail the desired contour, expected level of definition, waist, abdomen, buttocks, preference for a natural or more defined result, photo references, people cited, and surgical results admired or rejected.
Fears, questions, and perceived limitations should include spontaneous concerns about scar, pain, recovery, seroma, fibrosis, irregularities, thrombosis, grafting, buttock size, an artificial-looking result, return to the gym, time off work, and need for help.
Personal, social, and relationship context should record profession, children, partner, family support, self-esteem, body perception, relationship, social situations, gym, sports, travel, events, recovery availability, and postoperative support.
Clinical and surgical history should cover diseases, medications, hormones, GLP-1/GIP, supplements, allergies, smoking, alcohol, drugs, prior surgeries, complications, thrombosis, thrombophilias, healing/scarring, and other relevant data.
The physical exam of body contour should record only medical findings effectively described by region, including abdomen, flanks, back, buttocks, arms, thighs, and other relevant sites.
Medical-surgical analysis should relate anatomy, body composition, and skin quality to complaints and expectations, pointing out relevant anatomical limitations without turning subjective expectations into a diagnosis.
Procedures and alternatives discussed should be recorded only when mentioned, including liposuction, HD lipo, liposculpture, abdominoplasty, mini-abdominoplasty, diastasis repair, gluteal grafting, technologies, skin laxity treatment, and combined procedures.
Surgical planning should define liposuction areas, level of definition, abdominoplasty or mini-abdominoplasty, diastasis repair, scars, grafting areas and objectives, technologies, intraoperative ultrasound, and associated procedures, separating items that are defined vs. to be defined.
Preoperative optimization should record weight goals, weight stability, body composition, physical activity, smoking cessation, medication adjustments, exams, and discussed guidance.
Shared decision-making should document patient preferences, alternatives accepted or rejected, understanding of limitations, remaining questions, and decisions made.
Plan and pending items should record tests, weight loss, follow-up, evaluations, estimate, commercial contact, scheduling, and other action items.
Summary for future consultations should summarize who the patient is, main complaints, body description, desired result, central fears, relevant personal context, key findings, surgical strategy, and pending items.

name: Monitoring
author: Velum
description: Summarizes employment support interviews according to guidelines. Organizes health, progress, and intentions on a fact-based basis to assist in plan creation.
body:
Organize and summarize the "monitoring records for creating individual support plans" at employment transition support offices in accordance with the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare's recording guidelines.
Regardless of the order of speech, classify and organize according to the specified structure, and convert spoken language from polite to factual style.
Avoid subjective expressions and interpretations, and create records based on facts.
List three priority issues that the individual should achieve for employment.
Identify the individual's human strengths and abilities that can be utilized for employment.
Record the previously set support goals and policies, as well as the current status (achieved / ongoing / difficult, etc.).
Describe the effects and changes of the support content, and specific episodes or facts that serve as the basis for evaluation.
Record the user's health status (sleep, medication, meals, physical condition, etc.).
Record the user's mental stability and stress status.
Record the status of medical visits and the attending physician's opinions (if any).
Record attendance status (attendance rate, tendency to be late or leave early).
Record changes in the home or living environment (if any).
Record lifestyle rhythm and life management abilities (e.g., meals, money management).
Record progress in hard and soft skills (including communication) at the facility.
Record changes in hopes and motivations for employment.
Record the status of activities such as internships, applications, and interviews.
Record requests for support content, things the user wants to do in the future, concerns, and hopes or concerns about continued use.
Record other special notes (e.g., employment decision, family trouble, signs of interruption of use, etc.).
Separate and organize the user's "subjective opinions" and "objective facts".
Clearly indicate comparative evaluations with the previous time, and make records that can be used to review the support plan.
Write so that the current situation, goal progress, and support effects are clear.
Avoid abstract expressions and ambiguous wording, and write based on specific facts, actions, and statements.
If there are contradictions or discrepancies, record both contents and clearly state that there are differences.

author: Velum
description: Suitable for testing and R&D. Input requirements or API specifications to produce review points, test cases, and improvement suggestions.
body:
This article systematically elaborates on modern software testing lifecycle methodologies, covering all stages from requirements review to online operations, and emphasizing multi-dimensional quality assurance strategies such as automation, intelligence, security, performance, team building, and globalization.
Software testing is core to ensuring product quality, spanning the full lifecycle from requirements analysis to launch and operations. Early involvement in requirements and technical solution reviews promotes “shift-left testing,” preemptively avoiding design defects and API issues and reducing rework costs.
Test case design is the foundation of testing work. It should comprehensively cover positive, negative, boundary, and exception scenarios, align with real user flows, and be validated through joint reviews to ensure effectiveness. Test data preparation must ensure authenticity, diversity, and security, and leverage intelligent platforms to improve efficiency.
Automated testing is key to improving efficiency. Web UI automation should use frameworks like Playwright or Selenium to cover core flows. API automation should achieve 100% coverage of core APIs and be integrated into CI/CD pipelines to enable rapid feedback.
Mobile testing requires building a compatibility test matrix covering mainstream devices and systems and focusing on mobile-specific scenarios like network switching, permissions, and power consumption. Performance testing should establish a regular monitoring system, define performance baselines, and conduct specialized tests at key nodes to ensure system stability.
Security testing is a crucial barrier safeguarding product and data security. Use vulnerability scanning and penetration testing to uncover and fix security issues like SQL injection and XSS, and integrate security standards and processes into the entire R&D lifecycle to form a closed loop.
AI technology is driving a shift to intelligent testing. Large language models can assist in generating test cases, exploratory testing can reveal hidden defects, and AI can enable intelligent defect classification and script optimization to improve efficiency, depth, and breadth.
Online quality guarding extends testing work. Build real-time, end-to-end monitoring dashboards covering business, technical, and UX metrics, and establish P0/P1/P2 incident response mechanisms and postmortem processes for rapid response and continuous optimization.
Testing team capability building is core support for quality assurance. Establish a “newcomer-backbone-expert” three-level talent development system, provide systematic training and specialized improvement, and build innovation platforms. Accumulate knowledge assets to reduce talent dependence risk.
Global business expansion raises testing requirements. Build a test matrix across regions, networks, and languages, conduct compatibility and localization testing, ensure compliance with local data privacy regulations (e.g., GDPR, CCPA), and establish cross-region collaboration mechanisms.
Building a quality control system across the entire product lifecycle is critical. Set quality gates at requirements, design, coding, testing, launch, and operations, and build a comprehensive quality data dashboard to visualize R&D quality and drive continuous optimization.
The value of software testing lies in promoting product optimization, enhancing user experience and market competitiveness through full-chain quality control. Testers should continuously improve professional skills, embrace new technologies like AI, and strengthen cross-team collaboration to build high-quality software products.

name: DUQUE PLASTIC SURGERY
author: Velum
description: Submit the transcript and generate a structured and faithful anamnesis for the medical record. Useful for plastic surgery consultations.
body:
